instruct00424.title: Tin Can Roses
instruct00424.text: I wanted to do something special for my wife for our recent anniversary. Since her birthday was only 8 days previous and I went all out I was on a budget. I was not about to let an anniversary slip by without a memorable tribute so I got to work. I have a relatively unsophisticated collection of hand tools, no power tools to speak of and I'm not exactly overwhelmed with raw material choices around the house. After mulling over a bunch of ideas in my head over the course of a couple of days I decided on making her a dozen roses. I created them using pretty simple household stuff.Materials Needed: (6) Soda Cans (12) 11" pieces of constuction or strong craft wire (for stems)Tools Needed: Scissors (Don't use your wife's sewing scissors because they will be dull and worthless after cutting through tin cans.) Ballpoint Pen (Use a pen you don't care about because it will probably not write after this little adventure.) Sanding Sponge or Sand Paper Needle Nose Pliers (These will be used to cut and bend wire)Please Note: Be careful not to cut yourself on the sharp edges of the soda can. Thoroughly rinse the cans with hot water to keep them from getting sticky and gumming up your scissors. Once they're clean and dry cut off the tops and bottoms of the cans so only the sides remain. You can use a metal ruler to straighten out the material once you've cut the edges straight. Use a sanding sponge or plain old sand paper to thoroughly remove the paint from the surface of the metal. With a ballpoint pen that you don't need to ever use again and don't mind potentially destroying, trace a swirl shape from roughly the center of the material outward. The pen should make a little indentation in the material that you can use to cut out the final shape. Once you have your swirl shape go ahead and cut along the line you just drew. Using your crappy ballpoint pen, wind the material around the tip of the pen in a spiral. Try to keep the inside edge together as much as possible so you end up with more of a bloom shape. The idea is that surface should slant out from the bottom in sort of a coned spiral. At the base of the spiral you just created use a thumbtack to poke a little hole. this will be where you will poke the wire through for the stem. Try not to make the hole too close to the edge or the material may tear. This doesn't have to be perfect because it most likely will not be seen when the project is complete. Cut a piece of construction wire to about 2" longer then the final length you would like your flower stem to be. For my project I cut the lengths about 11". Using needle nosed pliers, wrap a small part of the end of the wire into a small bundle. This will help keep the shape of the bulb of the flower and also make a nice little bud in the center. Carefully thread the straight end of the wire down through the middle of the petals and through the small hole you made with the thumb tack, then bunch up the flower as tight as possible and wind a little curl in the wire to keep the bud nicely bunched together. Now you have your first rose. You can carefully bend and shape the metal at this point to make it look as much like a rose as possible. Once you have made all of the roses you can arrange them however you see fit and use a small piece of construction wire to bunch them together into an arrangement of a dozen, or just three to five if you're lazy. You can also use the scrap pieces left over from cutting out the swirls to make little leaves to attach to the stems.

# Structured Summary of DIY Soda Can Roses

## Inputs
- (6) Soda Cans
- (12) 11" pieces of construction or strong craft wire (for stems)
- Scissors (not sewing scissors)
- Ballpoint Pen (one that can be discarded)
- Sanding Sponge or Sand Paper
- Needle Nose Pliers
- Thumbtack

## Outputs
- A dozen handmade soda can roses

## Process
### START:
- Begin with the intention to create a memorable anniversary gift on a budget.

### PROCESS: Prepare Soda Cans
- Rinse the soda cans with hot water to remove stickiness.
- Cut off the tops and bottoms of the cans to isolate the sides.

### PROCESS: Flatten and Clean the Can Material
- Use a metal ruler to straighten out the sides of the cans.
- Sand thoroughly to remove paint from the metal surface.

### PROCESS: Create Swirl Shapes
- Trace a swirl shape from the center outward on the metal using a ballpoint pen.
- Cut along the indentation to produce the swirl shape.

### PROCESS: Form the Rose Petals
- Wind the metal swirl around the tip of the pen to create a spiral bloom shape.

### PROCESS: Prepare the Wire Stem
- Cut a piece of wire to approximately 13" (11" + 2").
- Use pliers to wrap one end of the wire into a small bundle.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the hole for the stem ready?
- IF YES: Proceed to thread the wire.
- IF NO: Use a thumbtack to poke a hole at the base of the spiral, then proceed.

### PROCESS: Assemble the Rose
- Thread the straight end of the wire through the hole.
- Bunch up the flower and twist the wire to secure the bloom.

### OUTPUT: First Rose Completed
- Shape the metal to resemble a rose more closely.

### DECISION [IF]: Are there more roses to make?
- IF YES: Repeat the swirl creation, petal forming, and assembly for each rose.
- IF NO: Proceed to arrange the roses.

### PROCESS: Arrange the Roses
- Arrange the roses into a bouquet using construction wire.

### DECISION [IF]: Do you want to add leaves?
- IF YES: Use scrap pieces to create and attach leaves to the stems.
- IF NO: Proceed to the end.

### END:
- The DIY soda can roses are completed and ready to be presented as a gift.
```

instruct00508.title: Better No-Cost Crampons
instruct00508.text: As winter rolled around, I got tired of slipping on icy pavement while getting to and from classes. I looked at purchasing a pair of inexpensive crampons, but the product reviews for most of them complained of the rubber pieces snapping. The nicer ones used spikes instead of chains, and I wanted something more low-profile. Essentially, I wanted crampons that were:Inexpensive to make low profile and without spikes, so that if I accidentally walked inside with them they would not scratch the floor Easy and quick to slip on and off so that I could effectively use them to get to and from class without being late because I had to put on crampons. So, I set out to make my own to meet my needs. I looked at a few instructables (and even attempted to make a few a while back, those weren't my best instructables) and came up with an even better design that combines these two instructables:https://www.instructables.com/id/Backpack-Cargo-Ne...https://www.instructables.com/id/No-Cost-Crampons/The finished crampons cost me nothing to make, and work great! You'll need:Old bike inner tube. I used a 26x1.95, but another size will do. You can often get old popped ones by asking nicely at bike shops. Scissors Nuts. You'll need about 20, and preferably they should be all the same size. Use your scissors to cut the tube into thin bands. Keep in mind that the bands must be thin enough to be threaded through your nuts. Don't cut the whole tube up though; you'll want to save some to cut into long strips for a later step. I won't explain how to weave the inner tube, but here's the instructable where I learned it from:https://www.instructables.com/id/Backpack-Cargo-Ne...the natural pattern of this weave is benzene-like hexagons, but you can make it into pentagons or squares, all depending on the shape of your foot. From time to time, put what you've woven so far on the sole of the shoe to see where you need to add more. Thread on the nuts where you want them. I put most up on the toes, and three on the heel.You'll want the loose ends of the bands to hang no more than about halfway over the edge of the sole; this will allow them to stretch over the top of your shoe, keeping them in place. Once you have your footprint all woven, cut a long strip of the inner tube, and loop it through all the loose ends of the bands. Then tie it off in a regular square knot. You'll want to be tight so that the whole thing "curls" up a bit, so that when you stretch it over your shoe it will be tight enough to hug the perimeter of your shoe. If you want, you can tie a strap over the top of the shoe. This will make the crampons stay on better, but will make them harder to put on. Now you're done with one of the crampons! Now just repeat the exact same thing for the other shoe. Now you have your own crampons for much cheaper, and arguably better quality, than if you had bought them from a store!Disclaimer: These are not guaranteed to keep you from slipping on ice; but rather a preventative measure. I am not responsible for any injury from the use of this instructable.

# DIY Low-Profile Crampons System

## Summary Representation

### START:
- Start the DIY crampon-making process.

### INPUT: Materials Required
- Old bike inner tube (26x1.95 or similar size)
- Scissors
- Nuts (approximately 20 of the same size)

### PROCESS: Prepare Materials
- Obtain an old bike inner tube from a bike shop.
- Use scissors to cut the tube into thin bands suitable for threading through nuts.

### STORE: Save Materials
- Reserve a portion of the inner tube to cut into long strips for later use.

### PROCESS: Weaving Technique
- Learn the weaving technique from an instructable (link provided in the blog).
- Weave the inner tube into a pattern that fits the shape of your shoe sole (hexagons, pentagons, or squares).

### DECISION [IF]: Check Weave Fit
- [IF] Is the weave fitting the sole of the shoe correctly?
  - [YES] Proceed to the next step.
  - [NO] Adjust the weave accordingly.

### PROCESS: Attach Nuts
- Thread nuts onto the weave at desired locations, focusing on the toe and heel areas.

### PROCESS: Trim Excess Material
- Ensure that the loose ends of the bands do not extend more than halfway over the edge of the sole.

### PROCESS: Secure Weave
- Cut a long strip from the saved inner tube.
- Loop the strip through all loose ends of the bands.
- Tie off the strip with a square knot, ensuring it's tight enough to cause the weave to "curl."

### DECISION [IF]: Add Top Strap
- [IF] Do you want to add a strap over the top for extra security?
  - [YES] Attach a strap over the top of the shoe.
  - [NO] Proceed without adding the strap.

### OUTPUT: One Crampon Completed
- Finish the first crampon.

### PROCESS: Repeat for Second Shoe
- Repeat the entire process to create a second crampon for the other shoe.

### OUTPUT: Pair of DIY Crampons
- Complete the pair of DIY crampons.

### END:
- End of the crampon-making process.

## Disclaimer
- The DIY crampons are a preventative measure and not a guaranteed solution to prevent slipping on ice.
- The creator of the instructable is not responsible for any injuries resulting from the use of these DIY crampons.
```

instruct00147.title: Shrimp & Spinach Penne Alla Vodka
instruct00147.text: This delicious dish incorporates fresh leafy spinach, wild caught shrimp, sun-dried tomatoes, a rich vodka sauce and your best sauvignon blanc. The dish itself has been known to put a stop to divorces, breakups and arrests. It has contributed to the happiness and well-being of countless couples and has helped spawn long-lasting friendships across the universe. If you're looking for a side to accompany this dish, my favorites are Italian-style bread with a roasted garlic spread or a side salad with a red wine vinegar dressing. If you want to top the dish, the best cheeses to use are a romano-parmesan blend or a thin-shredded mozzarella. So whether you are Giada, Paula, Rachael or Bobby, I encourage you to challenge me with a pasta that's better than this! Make sure you have all these ingredients on hand: 1 box of penne pasta 1 teaspoon of salt 15 large shrimp, peeled and deviened 1 bag of fresh, leafy green spinach 2 cloves of fresh garlic, minced 1/2 cup of sun-dried tomatoes, sliced into strips or chopped 1 cup of your best white wine 2 jars of Bertolli Vodka Sauce 2 tablespoons of olive oil 4 tablespoons of romano-parmesan cheese blend, divided Cooking Utensils 1 large pot 1 strainer 1 massive skillet 4 serving plates + 4 forks Bring water to a boil and dump in the whole box of pasta, adding just a teaspoon of olive oil and teaspoon of salt. Cook pasta according to package directions, but be sure that pasta is "al dente" While pasta is boiling, make sure that your garlic is minced and your sun-dried tomatoes are chopped or sliced. Then, coat the bottom of your massive skillet with two tablespoons of olive oil. Add the garlic and tomatoes and let cook for 1-2 minutes, letting the aroma fill your home. Once the garlic and tomatoes have cooked for 1-2 minutes, add the cup of white wine to the skillet along with your 15 shrimp. Allow 5 minutes for the shrimp to cook, and allow the wine to boil as it reduces. Once the shrimp are almost fully-cooked, add the whole bag of spinach to the skillet, letting it wilt. Once the spinach has wilted, add your 2 jars of pasta sauce, stir and let it simmer on low-med heat. Once the pasta has some bite to it, it's time to strain it. Strain all the water from the pasta and dump the pasta over the sauce in your massive skillet. Overlap the pasta over the sauce to combine the ingredients. Now, it's time to plate your dish. Put about 1-2 cups of your Shrimp & Spinach Penne Alla Vodka onto each of your four plates. Top with each portion with 1 tablespoon of parmesan-romano cheese. Now, it's time to cuddle-up to your loved one and share a romantic meal together. Mangia!

# Shrimp & Spinach Penne Alla Vodka Recipe Summary

## Ingredients
- 1 box of penne pasta
- 1 teaspoon of salt
- 15 large shrimp, peeled and deveined
- 1 bag of fresh, leafy green spinach
- 2 cloves of fresh garlic, minced
- 1/2 cup of sun-dried tomatoes, sliced or chopped
- 1 cup of white wine (preferably sauvignon blanc)
- 2 jars of Bertolli Vodka Sauce
- 2 tablespoons of olive oil
- 4 tablespoons of romano-parmesan cheese blend, divided

## Cooking Utensils
- 1 large pot
- 1 strainer
- 1 massive skillet
- 4 serving plates
- 4 forks

## Instructions

START:
1. PROCESS: Fill a large pot with water and bring it to a boil.
2. INPUT: Add the entire box of penne pasta to the boiling water.
3. INPUT: Add 1 teaspoon of olive oil and 1 teaspoon of salt to the pot.
4. PROCESS: Cook the pasta according to package directions until "al dente".

5. WHILE pasta is boiling:
    a. PROCESS: Mince the garlic and chop/slice the sun-dried tomatoes.
    b. PROCESS: Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a massive skillet.
    c. INPUT: Add minced garlic and sun-dried tomatoes to the skillet.
    d. PROCESS: Cook for 1-2 minutes until fragrant.

6. INPUT: Add 1 cup of white wine to the skillet.
7. INPUT: Add the 15 shrimp to the skillet.
8. PROCESS: Cook for 5 minutes, allowing the wine to reduce and shrimp to near full-cooked status.

9. INPUT: Add the entire bag of spinach to the skillet.
10. PROCESS: Let the spinach wilt.

11. INPUT: Add 2 jars of Bertolli Vodka Sauce to the skillet.
12. PROCESS: Stir and let the sauce simmer on low-medium heat.

13. DECISION [IF]: Is the pasta "al dente"?
    - YES: Proceed to step 14.
    - NO: Return to step 4 and continue cooking.

14. PROCESS: Strain all the water from the pasta using a strainer.
15. INPUT: Combine the strained pasta with the sauce mixture in the massive skillet.
16. PROCESS: Overlap pasta and sauce to mix the ingredients thoroughly.

17. PROCESS: Plate the dish by serving 1-2 cups of the Shrimp & Spinach Penne Alla Vodka onto each plate.
18. INPUT: Top each portion with 1 tablespoon of the romano-parmesan cheese blend.

OUTPUT:
- A romantic Shrimp & Spinach Penne Alla Vodka meal ready to be enjoyed.

END.
```

instruct00684.title: Industrial Pipe Bookshelf and Shoe Rack
instruct00684.text: This industrial pipe shelf is the perfect project for any handy -- or non handy -- person looking to update their room. The shelf is quick and easy to install and its hard industrial yet shabby chic look makes it a great addition to any room. All of the pipes have threaded ends which makes it really easy to update the shape of your shelf every few months.I've seen similar shelves on etsy of the same size starting at $150. I made this shelf myself for under $70. Materials (2) Flanges to mount pipe on the wall (8) Wood Screws - size 12x2" (8) 12" threaded pipes (1" diameter) (9) 90 degree pipe elbows (1" diameter) (2) 5" threaded pipes (1" diameter)Tools Hand drill Drill bits Pencil Measuring Tape Find a Stud: You want to mount the flanges on studs so you will need a stud finder to help you. I mounted my shelf in the corner of my room where I knew there would be a stud. Check out these resources for finding studs: How to Use a Magnet to find a StudStud finder pro iphone app Or buy one at your local hardware storeMount Flange: Once you have figured out where you want your shelf to be, decide where you want to mount the first flange and mark the holes with a pencil where you will drill. Drill pilot holes using a drill bit that is a bit smaller than the size of your screws. Hold the flange up to the wall and screw the flange in with the hand drill. Attaching the pipes is pretty straight forward. Screw the 5" threaded pipe into the flange. Attach an elbow pipe to the end and start adding the 12" pipes. TRICK: to get the pipes tight enough, after attaching the elbow pipes to the ends of the pipe, use the 2nd 5" pipe to tighten the connections. The 5" pipe gives you more torque, and is helpful when you need to tighten pipes near the corners. Attach the second 5" pipe to the second flange and attach an elbow pipe to the other end of the 5" pipe before attaching to the rest of the bookshelf. Determine where the flange will sit on the wall (should be in a stud, if not make sure to use dry wall screws) and mark the holes where the screws will go. Drill pilot holes using a drill bit that is a bit smaller than the size of your screws. Hold the flange up to the wall and screw the flange in with the hand drill. Lay your books upright or on their sides. It may take some time to balance the books, but I found that as long as the book on the bottom of the stack was stable it was easier to stack the rest of the books. I think any girl can appreciate how fabulous this shoe rack looks. I've always likes to display my shoes in my room (because I just love to stare at them). I used to have them on a wooden bookshelf, but the bookshelf was too clunky and took up WAY too much space in my room. Now that I've found this awesome solution I'm going to keep this pipe shelf to display my favorite shoes.

# Industrial Pipe Shelf System

## Summary
This system guides through the process of creating an industrial pipe shelf for home decor. It is designed for individuals who wish to add a stylish and functional element to their room. The system involves mounting flanges on wall studs, assembling pipes and elbows, and arranging books or shoes on the completed shelf.

## System Steps

### START:
- Begin the process of creating an industrial pipe shelf.

### INPUT: Materials and Tools
- (2) Flanges (1" diameter)
- (8) Wood Screws (size 12x2")
- (8) 12" threaded pipes (1" diameter)
- (9) 90-degree pipe elbows (1" diameter)
- (2) 5" threaded pipes (1" diameter)
- Hand drill
- Drill bits
- Pencil
- Measuring Tape
- Stud finder (or alternative methods to locate studs)

### PROCESS: Locate Wall Stud
- Use a stud finder or alternative method to locate a stud in the desired location for the shelf.

### DECISION [IF]: Is a stud found?
- Yes: Proceed to mount the flange.
- No: Use drywall screws appropriate for the wall type.

### PROCESS: Mount First Flange
- Decide on the location for the first flange.
- Mark the hole positions with a pencil.
- Drill pilot holes using a drill bit slightly smaller than the screws.
- Screw the flange into the wall with the hand drill.

### PROCESS: Assemble Pipes to First Flange
- Screw a 5" threaded pipe into the first flange.
- Attach a 90-degree elbow to the 5" pipe.
- Add 12" pipes to the elbow, using another 5" pipe for leverage to tighten connections.

### PROCESS: Mount Second Flange
- Attach a 5" pipe to the second flange.
- Attach an elbow to the 5" pipe.
- Determine the second flange position on the wall, ensuring it aligns with the first flange and is on a stud.
- Mark the hole positions with a pencil.
- Drill pilot holes using a drill bit slightly smaller than the screws.
- Screw the second flange into the wall with the hand drill.

### PROCESS: Complete Shelf Assembly
- Attach the assembled second flange and pipes to the rest of the shelf structure.
- Use the 5" pipe for additional torque to tighten all connections.

### OUTPUT: Finished Industrial Pipe Shelf
- The result is a mounted industrial pipe shelf ready for use.

### PROCESS: Arrange Books or Shoes
- Place books or shoes on the shelf.
- Ensure the bottom book or item is stable to support the rest of the stack.

### DECISION [IF]: Are books/shoes balanced?
- Yes: The arrangement process is complete.
- No: Adjust the positioning of items for stability.

### END:
- The industrial pipe shelf is now ready for display and use.

instruct00655.title: Wall Mounted Christmas Tree
instruct00655.text: I've always liked the idea of a wall mounted Christmas tree, especially because I live in a small apartment where floor space is at a premium. But most of the ones I've seen mounted on walls don't tend to look like real Christmas trees, which is what I wanted. So I came up with this idea to use pine garland to make a more traditional looking wall mounted Christmas tree. It's so easy to put up and I especially love the fact that there's no chance that my cat will topple it over, win-win! I used 3 pine garlands, each 9 ft long and 1 package of Glue Dots Flexible hang tabs to make the tree. I made a video of how I made the tree but I'll walk through the steps of how I made it here as well. I drew the outline of the tree with painters tape, and I made the base 3 ft wide. I used flexible hang tabsto hang the garlands, starting with the outline first, and then filling in the inside, fluffing up the garland to fill in the space. I decorated the tree just like you would a regular Christmas tree, with lights and ornaments. For the trunk, I used a scrap piece of 2"x3" and stained it. And I also made a rustic box with shimms and scrap wood to have a place to put presents. The flexible hang tabs are easily removable and won't damage the wall so the tree is easy to take down and store without taking up much space.

# Wall Mounted Christmas Tree System

## System Overview
The system is designed to create a wall-mounted Christmas tree that looks traditional while saving floor space. It is particularly suitable for small apartments and safe from pets. The system uses pine garlands, Glue Dots Flexible hang tabs, painter's tape, and additional decorations like lights and ornaments. It also includes creating a trunk and a rustic box for presents. The system is designed for easy setup and removal without wall damage.

## Process Steps

### START:
- Begin the wall-mounted Christmas tree creation process.

### INPUT:
- Gather materials: 3 pine garlands (each 9 ft long), 1 package of Glue Dots Flexible hang tabs, painter's tape, Christmas tree decorations (lights, ornaments), scrap piece of 2"x3" wood, shims, scrap wood, wood stain.

### PROCESS: [Draw Tree Outline]
- Use painter's tape to draw the outline of the Christmas tree on the wall.
  - Ensure the base of the tree is 3 ft wide.

### PROCESS: [Install Hang Tabs]
- Apply Glue Dots Flexible hang tabs along the outlined tree shape on the wall.

### DECISION: [Is Outline Complete?]
  - IF 'Yes' -> Proceed to fill in the inside.
  - IF 'No' -> Continue applying hang tabs until the outline is complete.

### PROCESS: [Hang Garland for Outline]
- Hang the first pine garland along the taped outline using the hang tabs.
  - Ensure it follows the contour of the tree shape.

### PROCESS: [Fill Tree Interior with Garland]
- Hang additional garlands inside the outline using more hang tabs.
  - Fluff up the garland to fill in the spaces and create a fuller look.

### PROCESS: [Decorate the Tree]
- Decorate the tree with lights and ornaments as desired.

### PROCESS: [Create the Trunk]
- Stain the scrap piece of 2"x3" wood to use as the tree trunk.
  - Attach the trunk to the wall beneath the garland tree.

### PROCESS: [Build Rustic Box]
- Construct a rustic box using shims and scrap wood to serve as a present holder.
  - Place the rustic box at the base of the tree.

### OUTPUT:
- The final output is a decorated, wall-mounted Christmas tree with a trunk and a rustic box for presents.

### DECISION: [Is Removal Needed?]
  - IF 'Yes' -> Proceed to removal steps.
  - IF 'No' -> END.

### PROCESS: [Remove Tree]
- Carefully remove the garland, decorations, trunk, and rustic box from the wall.
- Peel off the Glue Dots Flexible hang tabs without damaging the wall.

### PROCESS: [Storage]
- Store the garlands, decorations, trunk, and rustic box for future use.

### END:
- The wall-mounted Christmas tree creation and removal process is complete.

instruct00665.title: Ramen Burger
instruct00665.text: Making a ramen burger is easy, and the unusual noodle-y bun is sure to confuse and delight your taste buds; and your friends! The noodles are soft with great texture, and just like regular ramen noodles these noodle "buns" can be seasoned any way you like.Keizo Shimamoto created the ramen burger and shares all his ramen adventures on his blog. When he debuted the burger this year at a food fair in Brooklyn, NY people waited hours in long lineups for his original, noodle-y, twist on the classic burger. Now you can make your own ramen burger at home!All you need to make your own ramen burger buns are a pack of ramen noodles and an egg. 1 pack of ramen nooodles makes 4 "buns".Let's make a ramen burger! Open 1 package of ramen noodles and set included soup power aside. Place noodles into pot of boiling water, remove from heat and let soak for about 2 minutes. Strain water and let noodles cool completely, about 5-10 minutes. Once the noodles have cooled, crack an egg into the noodles and sprinkle in the soup powder. Gently mix until completely combined. To form the buns line any small round-bottomed dish with plastic food wrap. I used small disposable baking tins, but coffee cups or bowls without much taper also work well.Line the containers with plastic food wrap and scoop in a portion of noodles, then fold the plastic wrap over the noodle. I was able to stack my tins, and weighed them down with a large glass jar. The added weight from the jar will compress the noodles and help them keep a puck-like shape.Place the noodles and weight into the fridge for about 30 minutes. Set your range to high and heat up a frying pan. Add a drop of olive oil, then invert your noodle container into the frying pan. Let noodles cook for about 5-7 minutes and then carefully flip with a spatula. If your noodle puck is breaking apart allow to cook for another minute. Allow your noodles to cook the egg completely and get a nice golden brown colour.Don't worry if your first noodle bun doesn't turn out, it can take a few tries to get the buns to cook right. Practice makes perfect! The official recipe calls for green onion, arugula and soy sauce, but I went the classic bacon cheeseburger. Make your burger to suit your taste.Eating a ramen burger is an experience. instruct00311.title: Make Your Own Ferrofluid in 5 Minutes
instruct00311.text: Using magnetic ink and any oil lying around your house, make a substance that's liquid when it's sitting around, but turn solid in the presence of a magnetic field This instructable will show you how to make your own ferrofluid. A ferrofluid is a fluid with magnetic particles in it, and if the fluid is exposed to a magnetic field, all the magnetic particles will align with the field lines, and making the fluid much more dense. There's a lot of cool things you can do with this fluid. Enjoy!!! This is just about the simplest ferrofluid you can make. You'll need two basic materials: magnetic (MICR) ink, and a household oil. I've tried a couple types of oils, and it seemd like a light lubricating oil works best, but any cooking oil will work fine, as well. The amount of oil you have is pretty much the amount of ferrofluid you'll get out--about 50mL is good for starters, but feel free to make as much as you want. The ink is a dry magnetic ink that's used to print checks and other documents that use magnetic character recognition (check out the wikipedia article at http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_ink_character_recognition if you want to know more about this awesome technology). You can get a box of it on ebay for about thirty bucks (search for MICR or magnetic ink), and you can also get it at http://www.expresstonercartridges.com/okidata.htm. It's going out of style, so you'll have to poke around a little bit to find it. It's important to remember that you don't want a toner cartridge--just the toner. Pour some oil into a mixing cup. Add a bit of the ink, and stir it into the oil. You're making a suspension, so the ink won't dissolve in the oil. Just stir it. Keep on adding ink and stirring until you have a thick solution. There's no exact science to this. A good guideline for identifying a well-mixed fluid is that if you tip your mixing cup, the fluid should ooze rather than slosh. Grab your favorite permanent magnet and hold it up to the mixing cup (don't touch ithe fluid with the magnet, or even get close, unless you enjoy cleaning). Watch how the fluid turns from liquid to solid as you bring the magnet closer. Show your friends the horrible oily liquid you have in a cup, and then simulatenously slap a magnet onto it as you harmlessly 'dump' the cup over their heads (practice this first). Buy some cheap solenoids from http://www.allelectronics.com and electrically change the consistency of the fluid. Just enjoy! There's a lot of cool things people do with ferrofluid. You can make brakes with it by putting some fluid between a wheel's axle and hub. The wheel will spin freely as the fluid acts just as a liquid lubricant, but if you apply a magnetic field, you're suddenly putting a lot of friction of the wheel's rotation. The good folks at the Univeristat Der Kunste Berlin made a ferrofluid display that can play Nibbles: http://www.digital.udk-berlin.de/en/projects/winter0405/main/hauptprojekt/snoil.htmlI'm building on-the-fly braille translators and tactile interfaces by sensing if people are moving the fluid: http://www.artiswrong.com/ffb(just pictures and movies, no explanation/writeup yet....)

# Ferrofluid Creation System

## System Overview:
The system is designed to create ferrofluid, a substance that acts as a liquid under normal conditions but turns solid when exposed to a magnetic field. This is achieved by suspending magnetic particles in oil. The system takes magnetic ink and household oil as inputs and produces ferrofluid as the output.

### System Steps:

START: Begin the ferrofluid creation process.

INPUT: Gather the following materials:
- Magnetic (MICR) ink
- Household oil (light lubricating oil or cooking oil recommended)
- Mixing cup
- Stirring utensil
- Permanent magnet

PROCESS: Pour approximately 50mL of oil into the mixing cup.

PROCESS: Add a small amount of the magnetic ink to the oil.

PROCESS: Stir the ink into the oil to create a suspension. The ink will not dissolve but should be evenly distributed.

DECISION [IF]: Check the consistency of the mixture.
- IF the mixture oozes when the cup is tipped, [THEN] proceed to the next step.
- ELSE add more ink and stir, then return to the consistency check.

PROCESS: Once the desired consistency is achieved, test the ferrofluid by bringing a permanent magnet close to the mixing cup.
- DO NOT touch the fluid with the magnet or get too close to avoid a mess.

OUTPUT: Observe the ferrofluid turning from liquid to solid in the presence of the magnetic field.

PROCESS: Demonstrate the ferrofluid's properties to friends or use it in various applications such as:
- Simulating a harmless prank by pretending to pour the ferrofluid but using a magnet to solidify it.
- Purchasing solenoids to electrically control the consistency of the fluid.
- Exploring other creative uses like making magnetic brakes or ferrofluid displays.

END: The ferrofluid creation process is complete.
```

instruct00550.title: How to Make Crepe Paper Leis
instruct00550.text: Instructions on how to make leis out of crepe paper. Originally posted on my blog dreamalildream.com. Easy and great for Hawaiian themed parties. Crepe paper in rolls (or in folded sheets cut into 2 inch strips)Needle and Thread (I measured about 2 yards, but this depends on how long you want or need your lei to be&whatever you determine double it and thats your thread length)Scissors First measure your thread and cut it to size. Thread your needle and make the thread doubled so it is stronger than just one strand, and tie a knot at the end.Start hand sewing through the center of your crepe paper. You want to do about 1/4 inch stitches and pull your thread all the way through to the end as you go. Bunch up (like a fan) as you go. Once you have maybe an inch or more in length bunched, stop and twist clockwise, maintaining the tightness somewhat to keep the twirl. Keep going and repeat until you have reached the desired length of lei (on average it takes me an hour or so to do one). When you get to the end, sew into the beginning and knot off to connect the lei. Cut remaining thread and you're done! Enjoy! Good job. Here is what your finished lei should look like. :)

# How to Make Leis Out of Crepe Paper

## Structured Summary of the Blog Post Instructions

### START:
- Begin the process of making a crepe paper lei.

### INPUT: Gather Materials
- Crepe paper in rolls or folded sheets cut into 2-inch strips.
- Needle and thread (measure about 2 yards or as needed for lei length, then double this measurement for the thread).
- Scissors.

### PROCESS: Prepare the Thread
- Measure the thread based on the desired lei length, double it, and cut.
- Thread the needle with the cut thread, ensuring it is doubled for strength.
- Tie a knot at the end of the doubled thread.

### PROCESS: Start Sewing
- Hand sew through the center of the crepe paper strip.
  - Make stitches approximately 1/4 inch in length.
  - Pull the thread all the way through after each stitch.
  - Bunch up the crepe paper like a fan as you sew.

### DECISION [IF]: Check Bunch Length
- IF the bunched crepe paper is at least an inch or more in length:
  - OUTPUT: Proceed to twist the bunch.
- ELSE:
  - Continue sewing and bunching until the minimum bunch length is achieved.

### PROCESS: Twist the Bunch
- Once the bunch length is adequate, stop sewing.
- Twist the bunched crepe paper clockwise to maintain tightness and create the twirl effect.

### DECISION [IF]: Check Lei Length
- IF the lei has reached the desired length:
  - OUTPUT: Proceed to finish the lei.
- ELSE:
  - Continue sewing, bunching, and twisting until the desired lei length is achieved.
  
### PROCESS: Finish the Lei
- Sew the end of the lei into the beginning to connect it into a loop.
- Knot off the thread to secure the lei.
- Cut any remaining thread.

### OUTPUT: Completed Lei
- Enjoy the finished lei, which should have a twirled crepe paper appearance.

### END:
- The process of making a crepe paper lei is complete.
```

instruct00577.title: 35-cent Book Weight/Bookmark
instruct00577.text: If you, like me, are a big reader, you may have between one and five books going at once, on various subject matters, both fiction and non-fiction, both paper and e-book. Even if you don't love reading, you probably have to read paper books or magazines from time to time.Therefore, you know the value of good bookmarks, and I have even bought leather book weights in the past. These are great for holding books open while your hands are occupied. But they are bulky, and if you close a book with one inside and place any weight on top of the book, the binding can break.So I was excited to hear about the penny bookmark as described by Amy Sedaris in an interview when she was promoting her book Simple Times: Crafts for Poor People. The concept was simple: sandwich pennies between layers of packing tape, and you have an instant book weight and bookmark!I immediately made one for myself, and it quickly became my favorite reading tool. However, packing tape, even though it is pretty good quality, is not very durable, and before long, the pennies started wearing through. Plus the tape was slippery enough that if I picked the book up, the bookmark would slide right out. It was time for an upgrade.Having discovered the wonders of duct tape, I realized I could make a beautiful, functional book weight using the same concept. Not only that, but it serves these other purposes:What to do with those gazillion pennies you have lying around. You know, the ones where the metal is worth more than the coins themselves.It's an easy craft to do with the kiddos, either at home or in the classroom.Your Christmas/birthday/whatever gift needs have answered. These are awesome, and you can make them really pretty and cool looking. A recession-proof gift!Security. It's a great way to hide your stash of gold bullion from prying eyes if you need to.So here it is: the 35-cent* bookmark, your recession-proof, upcycled gift needs answered. You're welcome.*Cost is approximate and is based on 28 cents in pennies, and about 7 cents in everything else. You will need: Pennies (I raided my broken bookmark and my old bank for some) Duct tape Scissors Paint (optional) Other decorative stuff (optional) I used 14 rows of pennies. You can decide how long you want yours to be. If you read massive tomes, magazines or coffee table books, make it longer; mostly paperbacks, shorter. Remember, though, the expense will go up with the length! Lay the pennies side by side in rows of two on sticky-side-up duct tape. Carefully cover the duct tape strip with another one. You can use a contrasting color, if you like. Press the tape down so it seals on both sides. Trim the ends so they are even, and take off any part of the sides where sticky tape is showing. If you're just looking for a basic bookmark, you're finished! Now you can customize it any way you like. This is especially good if you are making yours as a gift, or if you just like to look at pretty things. I added silver tape to the ends of mine. instruct00465.title: Tying a Bow Tie Way # 2 (the Easy Way)
instruct00465.text: If you figured out how to tie a bow tie based on my previous instructable, this one should be a breeze. One of the main reasons that I do not use this method is that I have many bow ties that have different colored wings, and this method does not allow both colors or patterns to show on the final product. As you can see, the entire front of the bow tie is comprised of the striped pattern, and all of the polka dotted pattern is in the rear. Start out the same way as in my first bow tie instructable by placing the bowtie over your neck, polka dots on one side, stripes on the other. Once again, you are going to cross the striped side over the polka dotted side, and wrap it underneath like you would begin tying your shoe. Now, letting the striped side rest on your shoulder, create the bow shape with the polka dotted side. Here is where this method begins to vary from my other method.Bring the striped side of the bow tie down infront of the polka dotted bow, and continue to loop it up underneath and back ontop of the dotted side. (this loop should be inbetween your neck and all of the other material. This time, instead of making the second bow behind the first bow, we will make it infront, by pulling the striped section through the "big loop" we just made. Once again, pull a doubled over piece of the striped material through the loop, so the wing's loop is created. Make sure you don't pull too far, causing the flap of the tie to come thouugh the hole. Wiggle and waggle the ends of your bow tie so they look straight and neat. The end result should look something like the second picture here from the top. Congrats on learning to tie a bow tie! Hope my instructable was easy enough to follow.Remember to check out the alternate way to tie your bow tie too.

## Start

## Process Steps

PROCESS: Instead of creating the second bow behind, make it in front by pulling the striped section through the loop just created.
PROCESS: Pull a doubled-over piece of the striped material through the loop to form the wing's loop, being careful not to pull too far.

## Output

## End

instruct00094.title: Make a Remote Controlled Camera From a Cellphone!
instruct00094.text: Want to know what your cat is doing while at work? Send a text message to your newly made surveillance-cellphone and receive pictures and videos seconds later. Sounds like a dream? Not any more! This video explains how it works: A brave camera-cellphone (including SIM-card). I'm currently using a Sony Ericsson T630. A microcontroller (I use a Picaxe 18x) Solenoid relays Photoresistor (LDR) LED A few resistors might come in handy Wires Soldering iron Solder, cutters, tape etc. Oh, and another working cellphone. The idea is to replace your fingers with the relays and your brain with a microcontroller. Depending on how complex your phone is, i.e. number of different keys to press in order to send a picture, choose your microcontroller accordingly. My setup uses four outputs (four different keys on the phone) and one input on the microcontroller. It allows me to send a SMS text message (or call) to my hacked phone and it then cycles through the code, clicking its way through the menus, taking photos and returning them to me. I was optimistic about the joystick and quickly soldered up the wires. The joystick has up, down, left, right and center as possible connections. I had to crack open another joystick to figure out the connections. "Making a "right" or "left" requires many different pins to be connected in a certain manner and order, e.g; ""Right;"" First; yellow + black + blue + brown then; purple + orange I experimented and found that I could rationalize by always keeping some wires connected. This worked but made the joystick on the phone immobilized. For "Right" I ended up using two relays: on relay 2 on relay 1 pause off relay 1 off relay 2 Relay no.1 is the top left button on the key pad ("Select" and "capture"). Relay no.3 is the top right button on the key pad ( "more" and "send"). This is actually my first project involving a microcontroller. I recently acquired the Picaxe Experimenter board (and USB Programming Cable ) and I would highly recommend it for those interested in learning about micros. Let it be said; I'm a terrible coder and there are thousands of ways to do this better. The code is ugly but but it works and can be snatched below.The red standby-Led helps in confirming that the program is running:standby: high 5 pause 100 low 5 pause 300goto mainWhen a text or call is received a LED connected to the speaker output shines onto the LDR (light dependent resistor). The value is then read:readadc 2,b0 if b0 < 90 then standby if b0 > 90 then runThe start of the "run" command:run:wait 2 high 3 pause 100 low 3 pause 400wait 6 high 1 pause 100 low 1 pause 300 high 2 high 1 pause 100 low 1 low 2 pause 300 Why do I use relays? Well, I tried using transistors but my phone was so sensitive to stray voltages that I quickly opted for relays. The relays are actually great for this project because they give you a visual and audible confirmation at each step as the code is running. Another great advantage is the fact that you can interact directly by just tapping them. And besides, they look amazing don't they? The surveillance-phone works like a charm and there's no end to the possibilities of this device. I plan to monitor my dorm while away for the holidays. Please don't forget to rate me and be sure to visit my other Instructables!Have fun!

# Surveillance System Using a Modified Cellphone

## System Overview
The system enables the user to send a text message or call a modified cellphone, which then takes pictures and sends them back to the user.

### Components Required:
- START: A camera-cellphone with a SIM card (e.g., Sony Ericsson T630)
- INPUT: Microcontroller (e.g., Picaxe 18x)
- INPUT: Solenoid relays
- INPUT: Photoresistor (LDR)
- INPUT: LED
- INPUT: Resistors
- INPUT: Wires
- INPUT: Soldering iron
- INPUT: Solder, cutters, tape, etc.
- INPUT: Another working cellphone for sending commands

### Setup Process:

#### Preparing the Cellphone
- PROCESS: Open the cellphone and identify connections for the joystick (up, down, left, right, center).
- PROCESS: Solder wires to the joystick connections.

#### Configuring Joystick Connections
- DECISION: Is the action "Right"?
  - IF YES: Connect yellow, black, blue, and brown, then purple and orange.
  - IF NO: Go to the next action.

#### Wiring the Relays
- PROCESS: Attach two relays for the "Right" action.
  - OUTPUT: Relay 2 on, then relay 1 on, pause, relay 1 off, relay 2 off.
- PROCESS: Map the remaining relays for other required actions (e.g., "Select," "Capture," "More," "Send").

#### Connecting the Microcontroller
- PROCESS: Connect the microcontroller's outputs to the relays corresponding to the phone's keys.
- PROCESS: Connect the microcontroller's input to the photoresistor.

#### Programming the Microcontroller
- PROCESS: Write the code for the microcontroller to receive signals and control the phone.
  - SUBROUTINE [standby]: LED indication for standby mode.
  - SUBROUTINE [readadc]: Read the LDR value to detect incoming calls or texts.
  - SUBROUTINE [run]: Sequence of relay activations to navigate the phone's menu and send pictures.

#### Testing the System
- DECISION: Is the microcontroller code running correctly?
  - IF YES: Proceed to use the system.
  - IF NO: Debug and fix the code.

### Operating the Surveillance System:

#### Receiving the Command
- PROCESS: Wait for a text or call from the user's working cellphone.
- PROCESS: LED lights up in response to the phone's speaker output, which is detected by the LDR.

#### Executing the Command
- DECISION: Is the LDR value indicating an incoming command?
  - IF YES: Execute the "run" command.
  - IF NO: Return to standby mode.

#### Taking and Sending Pictures
- PROCESS: Follow the "run" command sequence to navigate the phone's menu.
- PROCESS: Take a picture.
- PROCESS: Attach the picture to a message.
- PROCESS: Send the picture to the user.

### End of the System
- END: The picture is received by the user's working cellphone, completing the surveillance process.
```

instruct00868.title: Lazy Latkes -- Quick Gluten-Free, Vegan Potato Pancakes
instruct00868.text: I feel like every year around Hanukkah, there's a sudden surge in potato pancake recipes on the internet. Most are made with flour, eggs, matzoh, eggs and whatever else but I find that usually the simplest approach is always the best -- culinary lex parsimoniae or something. This recipe contains only the most basic ingredients, yet still maintains all of the rich heartiness, crunchiness and yumminess of any other potato pancake recipe.It comes more-or-less from my family's age-old recipe for deruny/draniki.To Sum: Clean and puree a few potatoes, salt to taste and fry in oil. Even though I went ahead and made a page for each step, this is really what this recipe boils (or frys...) down to. You will NEED:Potatoes -- any kind are fine. I usually use Russets. 1 large potato per person is an OK way to gauge how many potatoes you'll need, but round up -- especially if you're a glutton like me.Salt -- just a dash, to taste.If you want to be decadent, you might also want one or some of these:Garlic -- I love garlic. I usually have to pause for a moment to convince myself to use only half of the garlic I want to use. 2-3 cloves is probably enough for most people.Spices -- Paprika is a safe bet, but feel free to experiment. Peel your potatoes and garlic. Use a blender, food processor or immersion blender to puree your raw peeled potatoes and garlic. Back in the day, the potatoes would have to be grated on one of the smaller sides of a box grater. If you don't have any of these modern conveniences, grating will still be perfectly fine provided you still grate them finely. Add salt and optional spices. Use a spoon to pour your pancakes into a hot pan with a thin layer of oil. The thinner you spread the batter the crunchier they'll be. Cook on medium heat for maybe 2 minutes per side, always making sure that there's plenty of oil. I've never been good at knowing how much time has passed so this is probably a better guideline: once you see the edges becoming crispy and brown, flip them over. Alternately, if you want to be a bit healthier you can just grill them on a griddle -- they'll be a lot less exciting though. When I was growing up these would always be served with sour cream, caramelized onions and crumbled bacon. Any of those toppings is amazing with these savory little things. A few years ago I joined the civilized world and started eating them with applesauce -- also tasty! I am about to eat this particular batch with some Ajvar, and that will probably be the best yet.

# Structured Summary of Potato Pancake Recipe

## Ingredients
- Potatoes (1 large per person, round up for extra)
- Salt (to taste)
- Oil (for frying)
- Optional: Garlic (2-3 cloves), Spices (e.g., Paprika)
- Optional toppings: Sour cream, Caramelized onions, Crumbled bacon, Applesauce, Ajvar

## Equipment
- Blender, Food processor, or Immersion blender (or a box grater if none of these are available)
- Frying pan or griddle
- Spoon

## Preparation Steps

### START:
- Begin with gathering all ingredients and equipment.

### INPUT: 
- Select the desired number of potatoes based on the number of servings.

### PROCESS: [Peel Potatoes and Garlic]
- Peel the potatoes and garlic cloves if using garlic.

instruct00438.title: Uni-Directional WIFI Range Extender
instruct00438.text: Easily receive WIFI signals from far away using a standard USB WIFI adaptor and a bit of ingenuity. This Simple idea requires no modifications to a USB WIFI adaptor or your computer. A simple way to increase the signal strength and range of your WIFI. Plus it works with all USB WIFI adaptors You need only a few parts for this project and they all are pretty cheap except for the USB WIFI adaptor. ( I got mine on sale for $10, just check the ads) 1 - Metal Strainer/Steamer 1 - USB WIFI Adaptor 1 - USB Extension Cable (I chose a 10ft long) " Drill Bit (I like to use stepper bits for metal) Gorilla Glue (Epoxy works well too) 2 - Zip Ties Remove the Center Post (If your's had one) and drill a 1/2" hole as that is perfect size to fit the usb extention. Insert the Female end of the USB extention (the part that doesnt connect to your computer) into the hole you just drilled. Then just apply the glue/epoxy and let it sit for 24 hours. This Creates a strong bond between the plastic and metal. I used some tape to help hold the connecter in place while the glue cured. Be sure to apply glue to both sides of the connecter. Once thats dry the next day, zip tie 2 of the metal "ears" so they wont fold in on themselves when you use it. Just plug the USB WIFI adaptor into the socket on the dish and plug the other end into your computer. Enjoy boosted signal strength and improved distance. Fire up Netstumber or Kismet to really see the gain in power. This works even better than I thought it would. Be sure to leave your comments on how well it worked. Works great for war driving too. I decided to make the dish tripod mountable as its really hard to try and hold it to lock in a far away signal. The parts needed are pretty straight-forward. Tripod Nut for the bolt on the tripod 9/32" Drill Bit (Stepper bit works really nice for enlarging the hole) Pick a hole near the edge of the dish and use the drill bit to enlarge it. I chose the one where one of the feet had once been secured. Then just put the bolt from the tripod trough the hole and secure with the nut. Works great.

# Summary: Enhancing WIFI Signal with a USB WIFI Adaptor and a Metal Strainer

## Steps to Increase WIFI Signal Strength

### START: Begin the process of enhancing WIFI signal reception.

### INPUT: Gather the required materials.
  - 1 Metal Strainer/Steamer
  - 1 USB WIFI Adaptor
  - 1 USB Extension Cable (10ft long recommended)
  - 1/2" Drill Bit (stepper bits recommended for metal)
  - Gorilla Glue or Epoxy
  - 2 Zip Ties

### PROCESS: Prepare the Metal Strainer.
  - [IF] Does the strainer have a center post?
    - [YES] Remove the Center Post.
    - [NO] Proceed to the next step.

### PROCESS: Drill a hole in the strainer.
  - Use the 1/2" drill bit to create a hole that fits the USB extension.

### PROCESS: Attach the USB Extension Cable.
  - Insert the Female end of the USB extension into the drilled hole.
  - Apply glue/epoxy to secure the connection.
  - Use tape to hold the connector in place while the glue cures.
  - Let the glue cure for 24 hours to ensure a strong bond.

### PROCESS: Secure the metal "ears" of the strainer.
  - Use zip ties to secure 2 of the metal "ears" to prevent them from folding.

### OUTPUT: Completion of the WIFI signal booster assembly.

### PROCESS: Connect the USB WIFI adaptor.
  - Plug the USB WIFI adaptor into the socket on the dish.

### PROCESS: Connect the assembly to the computer.
  - Plug the other end of the USB extension cable into the computer.

### OUTPUT: The system is ready to use.
  - Enjoy boosted WIFI signal strength and improved distance.

### DECISION [IF]: Is a more stable setup required for the dish?
  - [YES] Proceed to make the dish tripod mountable.
  - [NO] END: The process is complete.

### PROCESS: Make the dish tripod mountable (Optional).
  - INPUT: Additional materials needed.
    - Tripod Nut
    - 9/32" Drill Bit

  - Select a hole near the edge of the dish for mounting.
  - Use the 9/32" drill bit to enlarge the selected hole.
  - Insert the bolt from the tripod through the hole.
  - Secure the bolt with the tripod nut.

### OUTPUT: Tripod-mounted WIFI signal booster.

### END: The WIFI signal enhancement system is complete and operational.
```

instruct00215.title: Make Your Own Sodamix
instruct00215.text: So, you have a Sodastream and have just run out of Sodamix. You could always buy more, but what if you want to make flavors not offered by Sodastream? What if you want to save even more money? As you may have figured out by now, putting powdered drink mix into carbonated water doesn't work very well (unless you're going for a Diet-Coke-and-Mentos-style reaction). By saving your old Sodamix bottles, you can refill them with dissolved drink mixes and still use the measuring cap to make perfect soda every time. To make your own mixes, you will need: Empty Sodamix bottle Water Measuring cup with marks for milliliters Non-carbonated drink mix that makes 10 or 12 quarts You can start by cutting the old label off of the bottle. Most drink mixes will make either 10 or 12 quarts, and for the purposes of turning this into a soda "syrup," a quart is close enough to a liter. The Sodamixes originally came with 500 ml of syrup to make 12 liters. If your mix makes 12 quarts, fill your empty Sodamix bottle with 500 ml of water. If your mix only makes 10 quarts, then fill the empty Sodamix bottle with 420 ml of water. Now add all of the mix packets to the water, put the cap on, and shake until it's all dissolved. Now you can add your own label to the bottle, tape on the label from the drink mix canister, or leave them all blank and make mystery soda. Since your homemade Sodamix is the same strength as the original, you can still use the lines in the cap to measure. Enjoy!

- The process begins with the intention to create homemade Sodamix for use with a Sodastream machine.

2. Add all of the mix into the Sodamix bottle containing the measured water.
3. Secure the cap on the bottle.

## PROCESS: Dissolve the Mix
1. Shake the bottle until the drink mix is fully dissolved.

## PROCESS: Label the Sodamix Bottle
1. Create a new label for the bottle, or
2. Tape the label from the drink mix canister onto the bottle, or
3. Leave the bottle unlabeled for mystery soda.

## OUTPUT: Homemade Sodamix Ready for Use
- The result is a homemade Sodamix solution, ready to be used with a Sodastream machine.

## PROCESS: Use the Homemade Sodamix
- Use the lines in the Sodamix bottle cap to measure the correct amount of syrup for carbonating with the Sodastream.

## END:
- The process concludes with the enjoyment of homemade carbonated beverages using the Sodastream machine.

instruct00672.title: Rainbow Loom: Starburst
instruct00672.text: This starburst bracelet is fun and (somewhat) easy. I hope that you will enjoy this *step by step* instructions. The materials that you will need are:Your loomYour hook or a crochet hookThree or more colours of elasticsC or S clip Take your first colour and place it from the center peg out to the left and right pegs.Now take the same colour and place it on the outside left peg. Do the same to the right side.Then take your outside colour and place it all the way up on both outside pegs. Remember to push the bands down! Take your second colour and start at the second peg in the middle. Now bring it out to the second right peg. Do the same thing but bring it out to the first right peg. So basically in a clock wise direction. Now reapeat step 3 all the way up until the end. Switch colours if you want to. With the same colour you did the starbursts, make a figure eight. Now place it over one the other side. Also place another capping band on the end with your outside colour. Turn your loom around and get under the first starburst capping band and get the first rubber band. Next get under the capping band and grabbing the first band again. Now reapeat that step: Always grab the first band and pull it where it belongs. Pull the different colour forward.(see the last two pictures) :) Get under the capping band and get the last band and bring It to where it goes. Now on the left side get your outside colour and hook it forward. Do the same on the other side. Now that you are done hooking we are going to add an extension. Take the last peg and stick your hook through the peg. Take a band (same colour as your outside) and put it on the hook.Now pull it through. You may need an adult to help. Once that is complete you can take off the bracelet. Now take your outside colour and put some bands on the loom(look at first picture). Take the elastic band that's on your hook and place it on the last two pegs. To end the bracelet look at the rest of the pictures. Hope you enjoyed and remember to press favourite.:)

# Starburst Bracelet Creation System

## Inputs:
- Loom
- Hook or crochet hook
- Three or more colours of elastics
- C or S clip

## Process:

START:
  - Begin with setting up the loom, hook, elastics, and clip for use.

PROCESS [Set initial bands]:
  - INPUT first colour of elastics.
  - Place the first band from the center peg out to the left and right pegs.

PROCESS [Create outside rows]:
  - Place the same colour band on the outside left peg.
  - Repeat the same process for the outside right peg.

PROCESS [Fill outside pegs]:
  - Take an outside colour and place bands all the way up on both outside rows of pegs.
  - Push the bands down as you go.

PROCESS [Create starbursts]:
  - INPUT second colour of elastics.
  - Starting at the second peg in the middle, stretch the band out to the second right peg.
  - Repeat the process, stretching the band out to the first right peg in a clockwise direction.
  - Continue this pattern up the loom until the end.
  - DECISION [Switch colours for starbursts]:
    - IF Yes:
      - Switch to a different colour of elastics for subsequent starbursts.
    - ELSE:
      - Continue with the same colour.

PROCESS [Add capping bands]:
  - With the same colour used for starbursts, make a figure eight with a band.
  - Place it over to the opposite side.
  - Add another capping band on the end with your outside colour.

PROCESS [Turn loom]:
  - Turn the loom around to start hooking process.

PROCESS [Begin hooking]:
  - Get under the first starburst capping band and hook the first rubber band.
  - Repeat the hooking process for each capping band, always grabbing the first band and pulling it to its corresponding peg.
  - Pull the different colour bands forward as shown in the last two pictures.
  - Get under the capping band, grab the last band, and bring it to where it belongs.

PROCESS [Hook outside rows]:
  - Hook the outside colour bands forward on both sides.

PROCESS [Add extension]:
  - Stick the hook through the last peg.
  - INPUT a band of the same colour as the outside.
  - Pull the band through with the hook.
  - DECISION [Need an adult's help]:
    - IF Yes:
      - Request assistance from an adult.
    - ELSE:
      - Continue to the next step.

PROCESS [Remove bracelet]:
  - Carefully remove the bracelet from the loom.

PROCESS [Create extension on loom]:
  - Place some bands of the outside colour on the loom as shown in the first picture.
  - Place the elastic band from the hook onto the last two pegs.

PROCESS [Finish the bracelet]:
  - Refer to the rest of the pictures for finishing the bracelet.

OUTPUT:
  - Completed starburst bracelet.

END.
```

instruct00678.title: Surfboard Repair
instruct00678.text: I put my elbow through the bottom of my board. The ding was 2" by 3" and about 1/2" deep. The nose and tail had a few other dings from a road trip I had gone on. The plan:My plan was to fill the hole with q-cell foam then put a layer of fiberglass cloth. Something to keep in mind is how you want the patch to look. This board is an old beater it has been patched more than a few times, so color matching wasn't super important to me. Tools: sand paperknife/ box cutter ragmixing sticks Materials:Resin (sun cure)fiberglass cloth Q-cell foam Start by prepping the ding. Grab some rough sandpaper 80-100 grit then sand any of the damaged area. The resin needs a rough area to bond with and splinters in the old glass will leave air pockets. Mix the Q-cell powder with the resin. You want the consistency thick (somewhere between toothpaste and play dough). When mixing or applying the resin It works best to do it in a closed garage or another place that doesn't have a lot of UV light coming in (make sure where ever you are working has good ventilation). The resin I was using is UV activated, so you can only put this stuff on around a 1/4" at a time. Let is sit for 5 min in the sun and it will cure it. Put on as many layers as you need then sand it down smooth. You want to sand the new foam to be flush with the rest of the board. I used the mix stick to try a few different shades of yellow. I ended up using a old yellow sharpie on the new foam. After the the foam is sanded down lay cloth on and cut it to size. I usually cut it so there is 3/4 of an inch over the edge of the patched area. Put some resin down and spread it around then lay the cloth on top of it. Spread it around and make sure there are no air bubbles. Add more resin on top and spread it evenly. Then sand it smooth. Make sure you don't go to deep and weaken the fiberglass you just put on. I usually will put a second layer of resin then light sand it with 200 grit. If it still isn't smooth repeat till it is. Finally wet sand it with 400 grit. If you don't want to color match it have fun. I just grabbed this stencil on google, I felt like the best way to cover a big white patch was a big white storm trooper helmet.Let me know if you have any questions or have any tips.

# Surfboard Repair System

## Summary Representation

### START:
- Begin the surfboard repair process.

### INPUT:
- Gather tools: sandpaper, knife/box cutter, rag, mixing sticks.
- Gather materials: Resin (sun cure), fiberglass cloth, Q-cell foam.

### PROCESS: Prep the Ding
- Use rough sandpaper (80-100 grit) to sand the damaged area.
  - **OUTPUT:** A roughened area that allows resin to bond effectively.

### PROCESS: Mix Q-cell Foam and Resin
- Mix Q-cell powder with the resin to a thick consistency, similar to toothpaste or play dough.
  - **STORE:** The mixture for application.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the workspace UV-light controlled and well-ventilated?
- **Yes**: Proceed to apply the mixture.
- **No**: Find an appropriate workspace before proceeding.

### PROCESS: Apply the Mixture
- Apply the resin and Q-cell mixture in layers, each approximately 1/4" thick.
  - **OUTPUT:** Filled hole in the surfboard.

### DECISION [IF]: Does the mixture need more layers?
- **Yes**: Add another layer and cure in the sun for 5 minutes.
- **No**: Proceed to sanding.

### PROCESS: Sand the Foam
- Sand the new foam until it is flush with the rest of the board.
  - **OUTPUT:** A smooth, level repair area.

### INPUT:
- Choose a color or design for the patch (optional).

### PROCESS: Color Matching (Optional)
- Test different shades of yellow with a mix stick or use a yellow sharpie to color the new foam.
  - **OUTPUT:** Colored foam that matches the rest of the board.

### PROCESS: Cut and Apply Fiberglass Cloth
- Lay the fiberglass cloth over the repaired area and cut it, leaving an extra 3/4 inch around the patch.
- Apply resin to the board, place the cloth over it, and ensure there are no air bubbles.
  - **OUTPUT:** Fiberglass cloth secured over the patch.

### PROCESS: Apply Final Resin Layers and Sand
- Add more resin over the cloth and spread it evenly.
- Sand the area smooth, being careful not to weaken the new fiberglass.
  - **OUTPUT:** A smooth and reinforced repair.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the repaired area smooth?
- **Yes**: Proceed to final sanding.
- **No**: Apply another layer of resin and sand again.

### PROCESS: Final Sanding
- Lightly sand the repaired area with 200 grit, then wet sand with 400 grit for a smooth finish.
  - **OUTPUT:** Fully smoothed and finished repair.

### INPUT:
- Select a design or leave the patch as is (optional).

### PROCESS: Apply Design (Optional)
- Apply a stencil design, such as a stormtrooper helmet, to cover the repaired patch.
  - **OUTPUT:** Aesthetically finished repair.

### END:
- The surfboard repair process is complete.

instruct00056.title: How to Clean and Re-wax a Surfboard
instruct00056.text: What's the matter? Got sand in your wax? The main problem with surfing, apart from the fact that it is almost impossible, is that you get sand in your wax, which turns your board into a manually operated belt sander, especially as you duck dive under waves. This is not such a problem in cold places, because you wear a nice long wetsuit. But in warmer spots, your legs/knees with soon resemble a raw souvlaki column. This instructable tells you how to clean the old wax off, and put new stuff on! This board has just been cleaned. There are a number of different ways you can clean the old wax off, but the best way, I think, is to leave it in the sun to let the wax soften, then scrape off with a board scraper (that I lost) or your driver's license (that I haven't lost). The license works better. You can remove the last of the wax by rubbing the board with a rag soaked in turps (turpentine). I've heard that Vaseline also works well for removing wax, but it's not as instant as turps and the fumes don't make you giggle as much as turps. If you are doing this on concrete, put something like a towel under your board... Choosing your wax! There are all different kinds of board wax to suit different water temperatures. Where I live, the water is about 22C at the moment, so I use Sexwax 3x cold water soft "Quick Humps". I'll leave that there. There's a big difference in types of wax, in warm water you want thicker wax, in California you can just about dip your board in diesel and have it wax up. Ask the surly guy with his pants halfway round his arse in the surfshop what to use for your local area. Now, rub the block of wax across your board, and then lengthways over the same area. Pay special attention to the rails - it's not considered 'cool' to have lots of wax on your rails because in theory it cuts down your speed on the wave. However, this is like worrying about the wall paper on the space shuttle. The only people who are good enough to notice a reduction in board speed have an army of groupies to wax their board for them. For regular surfing mortals, wax on the rails means you can hold and push the board down for duck diving - if your hands slip off during this process you cop a board in the face, 'Sticky rails to you, till we meet again' etc. So: sticky rails is nice rails. A note on board wax: There are good places to keep board wax and bad places to keep board wax. The dashboard falls into the second category. See pic. So this is what it should look like - you should have lumps of wax all over your board. It should resemble bad 70's wallpaper, but sticky. More lumpy is better. Right, now go get wet!

instruct00051.title: DIY AquaPod Made From PPR Pipe
instruct00051.text: This is made from PPR pipe (polypropylene).I intend to use this for my SJcam action camera underwater 1) 1 length - 25mm diameter PPR pipe. Length depends on your preference. I ended up with 30cm long pipe which could fit on my scooter u-box.2) 2 pcs - end cap of the same size3) 1 pc - bolt which I salvage from broken monopod for smartphone You may use bolt or screw from hardware but it should not be pointy.4) Adapter which is included from my action camera 1) Drill one end cap on center so as the bolt could fit snugly. This is to avoid water ingress when your aquapod is used underwater.2) Insert the bolt just the ideal length that the adapter will fit in. You may put sealant around the bolt to add more "water resistance".3) Heat one end of the pipe at a time then place the end cap firmly. Do the same on the other tip. I used stove to melt the tip of pipe a bit. If you have PPR fusion machine you may use it. 4) Place the adapter and you're good to go with your new aquapod.

# Structured Summary of DIY Aquapod for Action Camera

## Inputs:
- 1 length of 25mm diameter PPR pipe (30cm long)
- 2 pcs of end caps (same size as the pipe)
- 1 pc of a bolt (salvaged from a broken monopod or sourced from hardware)
- 1 action camera adapter (included with the camera)
- Sealant (optional for additional water resistance)
- Tools for drilling, heating, and assembling

## Process Steps:

### START:
- Begin the construction of the DIY aquapod for an action camera.

### INPUT:
- Gather all required materials and tools.

### PROCESS [Drill End Cap]:
- Drill a hole in the center of one end cap to fit the bolt snugly, ensuring water resistance.

### DECISION [IF Bolt Fits Snugly]:

### PROCESS [Prepare Bolt]:

### DECISION [IF Sealant is Used]:
  - **IF YES:** Apply sealant around the bolt for extra water resistance.
  - **ELSE:** Continue without applying sealant.

### PROCESS [Heat Pipe End]:
- Heat one end of the PPR pipe using a stove or a PPR fusion machine if available.

- Repeat the heating process for the other end of the PPR pipe.

### PROCESS [Attach Second End Cap]:
- Attach the second end cap to the other heated end of the pipe.

### PROCESS [Attach Adapter]:
- Place the action camera adapter onto the bolt protruding from the end cap.

### OUTPUT:
- The completed DIY aquapod is ready for use with an action camera underwater.

### END:
- The construction process of the DIY aquapod is complete.

instruct00713.title: How to Make Delicious Scrambled Eggs
instruct00713.text: I made these delicious scrambled eggs this morning. It is a simple and quick recipe which produces great tasting scrambled eggs! Here is what you will need to make these delicious eggs.Eggs I made threeSaltPepperCanola Oil SprayButterMilkPanSpatulaBowlForkKnife Crack open the eggs into a bowl. I crack the egg against the bottom or side of the bowl, because it reduces the chance of egg shell getting into the egg. Now take a fork to crush the yolk and make a smooth mixture where the yolk and egg white are mixed together. You can also use a whisk to do the job, but I have more success with a fork in a smaller bowl. With the eggs in your bowl, add some preliminary ingredients. I add some salt and pepper. I usually like more pepper, but it is your preference. You can also add some milk or water to make it more creamy. I added milk, just because I love it in my eggs. Now it is time to prep the pan that you will scramble your eggs on. I first spray it with Canola Oil to reduce the amount of sticking the eggs have against the pan. Then I get a knife and put some butter on it, a little less than the amount you use to butter your bread. I rub the butter around the pan to add some flavor to the eggs. Pour the egg blend on to the pan, and let it sit for a couple of seconds. Now take your spatula and start to scrape around. Scatter the eggs, spread them out, bring them together, scramble them! Add some more salt or pepper if you like. That is what I do, and I also add some milk to the pan during the scrambling. Pour the eggs onto a plate and serve to yourself, or to whom ever you made them for! Make sure you cleanup afterwards too! Eggs can sometimes be a pain to clean off of a pan, so don't procrastinate! Enjoy!

# Scrambled Eggs Recipe System

## Ingredients and Utensils:

instruct00743.title: Rust Dyeing
instruct00743.text: Rusty metal is a really interesting material to dye with. It produces a warm orange and brown color and you can make patterns with it. Take a look how I dyed fabric with rusty sheets! To dye the fabric with rust, you need:- Salt - A spray bottle - White vinegar - Fabric (natural fabrics made from, for example, cotton and linen work the best) - Rusty objects The first step is to spray a combination of water and white vinegar on the fabric with the spray bottle. It's important that the fabric is all wet. The white vinegar will speed up the process of the rust coming of the metal and go into the fabric. To dye the fabric I'm using rusty sheets. By folding the fabric over the plates and put new plates on top I covered the whole piece of fabric. Make sure the fabric stays wet by spraying water and vinegar on the fabric and rusty objects. You can sprinkle some salt over the metal and fabric, salt has the similar effect on rust as the white vinegar.Make sure the rusty metal is pressing on the fabric by putting some heavy weight objects on top op de metal. After a couple of minutes the textile is already absorbing the rust. Try to be patient and wait at least a day/night before you remove all the rusty objects from the fabric. After a day or night of absorbing, you can see a pattern of brown, orange and even green colors. Remove all the rusty objects and see the result! To fix the pattern on the fabric and stop the rusting process, you need:- Container or bucket filled with hot water - Salt - Spoon Create a fixing bath by dissolving a spoon of salt in the bucket with hot water. Use this bath to rinse the fabric and to fix the rusty pattern. I used two fixing baths and also rinsed the fabric twice with clean water, without salt. Let your dyed fabric dry. Let the rusty objects also dry, so you can reuse them.The fabric is now ready to use! Check out my Instructable about making a Rust Dyed Tote Bag: www.instructables.com/id/Rust-Dyed-Tote-Bag!

- Rust-dyed fabric with a pattern

- PROCESS: Fold the fabric over the plates and layer more plates on top to cover the entire fabric.

### PROCESS: Maintain fabric wetness
- OUTPUT: Fabric and rusty metal kept moist with vinegar solution.

### PROCESS: Add salt to enhance rusting
- INPUT: Sprinkle salt over the metal and fabric.

### PROCESS: Apply weight

### DECISION [IF]: Has the fabric absorbed the rust for at least a day/night?
- IF Yes: Proceed to remove the rusty objects.
- IF No: Continue to wait and maintain wetness as needed.

### PROCESS: Remove rusty objects
- OUTPUT: Fabric with a rust-induced pattern.

### PROCESS: Create the fixing bath
- INPUT: Dissolve a spoon of salt in hot water in a container or bucket.

### PROCESS: Rinse the fabric in the fixing bath
- OUTPUT: Rust pattern on the fabric is fixed.

### PROCESS: Rinse the fabric with clean water
- OUTPUT: Excess salt and vinegar are removed.

### PROCESS: Dry the fabric
- OUTPUT: Rust-dyed fabric ready to use.

### PROCESS: Dry the rusty objects
- STORE: Rusty objects are dried for reuse.

### END:
- The rust dyeing process is complete.

instruct00856.title: Functional Steampunk Airsoft Pistol
instruct00856.text: When I saw the Steampunk Challenge it gave me the motivation to actually do this project which had been kicking around in my head for a while. I have a bunch of less-than powerful Airsoft guns lying around, a bunch of random junk, adhesives, and metallic paint. Combine all of this, and I get a Steampunk Airsoft gun! I also wanted the gun to work. Maybe not be easy to cock, or load, or aim, but at least fire. This one fits that description perfectly. This gun is not up to my personal artistic standards, but I couldn't figure out something to edge the leather with to my satisfaction, or something to cover the exposed glued woods on the ends of the scope. Without further ado, here is my Steampunk Airsoft gun. The gun I chose had some accuracy issues so i decided to to take it apart and maybe fix that. I found the problem- a cracked barrel mount- and patched it up with Krazy Glue (CA glue). That fixed it wonderfully

instruct00261.title: Make Your Own Roll-Up Keyboard
instruct00261.text: Have you ever wanted one of those pricy roll up keyboard but didn't want to spend the money? Here is a quick and dirty way to make your own. For this project you will need: 1 USB Keyboard 1 Screw driver with interchangable bits Handful of small project sized nuts and bolts Using the screwdriver deconstruct the keyboard. Remove the keyboard's membrane switch pad and control board. The membrane consists of 3 separate layers tacked together. Using the rubber pad, plate and nuts & bolts, reassemble the membrane to the control board. Make sure that the traces of the membrane line up with the traces on the control board. If your keyboard had a socket and ribbon cable just reinsert the cable and you ready to label the keys. After the long process of labeling the keys you are now ready to use your roll up flexible keyboard. Using a text editor check to make sure all your keys function. HINT: to save time label only the keys you use most, or learn to touch type :)
