```markdown
# Custom Skateboard Mold Design Process

## Preparation

START:
- Gather all necessary tools and materials.

INPUT: Tools and Materials Needed
- Utility knife with a sharp long blade
- A saw (Japanese saw or a regular saw)
- Rasp or surform
- Foam sanding block (made from a block of foam, wider than the width of the deck, with 100 grit sandpaper or grip tape glued to one side)
- Pencil or black marker
- Straight edge (combination square or 12" ruler)
- Mold material (foam, MDF, or other stable, shapeable material)

## Design Layout

PROCESS:
1. Lay out the design features on the mold material using a pencil or black marker. This includes concave, kick/nose tails, and drops.

## Cutting the Mold

PROCESS:
2. Use the utility knife to make a series of cuts across the foam, approximately 1" apart, just above the depth of the side profile line.
   - Ensure not to cut below the profile line.

PROCESS:
3. Use the saw to cut above the profile line. If a saw is not available, use the utility knife blade turned on its edge.

PROCESS:
4. Remove the excess pieces of foam after cutting. The appearance may be messy at this stage.

## Shaping the Mold

PROCESS:
5. Begin shaping the concave into the foam using a surform, being careful not to shape past the concave lines drawn.
   - Keep the profile flat between the two lines for optimal vacuum veneering.

PROCESS:
6. Extend the top line of the deck to the edge to create an even curve, about 1" inset into the foam.

PROCESS:
7. Feather the edge with the surform to create a gradual transition.

PROCESS:
8. Use the straight edge to check the flatness of the concave profile periodically.

## Sanding the Mold

PROCESS:
9. Sand the mold using the flat sanding block, moving crossways (90 degrees to the length of the deck) to maintain flat planes.
   - Do not sand below the template lines on either side of the mold.

PROCESS:
10. Continue to check the flatness with the straight edge frequently during sanding.

PROCESS:
11. Finish the surformed concaves by sanding to the line and no further to avoid over-sanding.

OUTPUT: The finished mold should have nose, tail, and concaves shaped uniformly, with the drawn template lines still visible.

## Conclusion

END:
- The skateboard mold shaping process is completed, ready for the pressing of the skateboard deck.
- A few images of the pressing process and the final deck are provided for reference.

Courtesy of Ted from Roarockit.
```

instruct00204.title: How to Put Together a Skateboard
instruct00204.text: This will show you how to put together a skateboard.I do suggest you at least wear a helmet because i recently was bombing a hilll and got speed wobbles and my head made contact first and i think i got a little dumber cause i can hardly talk Materials: .skateboard .2 trucks .4 wheels .8 bearings(all in a pack) .8 nuts and bolts (all in pack) .griptape .riser pads(optianal) .13mm socket .16mm socket .3/8 wrench .socket wrench .drill with philips bit or philips screwdriver Unpeel grip tape and set the tips on the banked part of the board. Slam your hands down in the middle and work your way to the sides leaving no bubbles. Take a screw driver and rub the edges down so it outlines the board. Take a razor blade on the outlines area of the board at 45 degrees and cut all around the board. Cut off all the excess griptape. First insert all the bolts into the little holes making sure the head is on the griptape. Attach the trucks by sliding the bolts into the little holes on the truck and make sure the main bolt is facing torward the middle of the board. Now screw on all the little nuts onto the bolts by holding the bolts in place with the 3/8 wrench. Using the drill, drill the bolts so the nuts will slide up. Take bearing and push it into the wheel as far as possible with your hand and then take the largest socket you have and position it so the ring of it so its on the outer ring of the bearing. Take the hammer and hammer the socket until the bearing is in. Once you have that done insert your bearing spacer. Then you repeat it on the other side and all your wheels. Remember be gentle when putting in the bearings they are what makes your board roll. First remove the bolt and one washer then take a wheel and stick an allen wrench or screw driver in the bearing hole and wiggle it around until the wheel falls down the screwdriver. Once you have done that slide the wheel onto the axel of the truck then slide the washer on the axel and bolt in the nut. Repeat with other wheels. Now you have succesfully(hopefully) put together a skateboard. Now get out and go skate.

```markdown
# Skateboard Assembly System

## START:
- Begin the process of assembling a skateboard.

## INPUT: Gather Materials
- Skateboard deck.
- 2 trucks.
- 4 wheels.
- 8 bearings (all in a pack).
- 8 nuts and bolts (all in a pack).
- Griptape.
- Riser pads (optional).
- 13mm socket.
- 16mm socket.
- 3/8 wrench.
- Socket wrench.
- Drill with Philips bit or Philips screwdriver.
- Razor blade.

## PROCESS: Apply Griptape
1. Unpeel the griptape.
2. Align and set the tips on the banked part of the skateboard deck.
3. Press down in the middle and work towards the sides to eliminate bubbles.
4. Use a screwdriver to rub the edges to outline the board.
5. Cut the griptape along the outline at a 45-degree angle using a razor blade.
6. Remove excess griptape.

## PROCESS: Install Trucks
1. Insert bolts through the deck holes with heads on the griptape side.
2. Place trucks onto the bolts, ensuring the main bolt faces the center of the board.
3. Secure nuts onto the bolts using the 3/8 wrench to hold bolts in place.
4. Tighten the nuts with a drill or socket wrench.

## PROCESS: Install Bearings into Wheels
1. Push one bearing into a wheel with your hand as far as possible.
   - DECISION [IF]: Is the bearing fully inserted by hand?
     - Yes: Proceed to step 2.
     - No: Use a hammer and the largest socket to press the bearing in by hitting the socket.
2. Insert the bearing spacer into the wheel.
3. Repeat the process for the other side of the wheel and for all wheels.

## PROCESS: Attach Wheels to Trucks
1. Remove the nut and one washer from a truck's axle.
2. Insert an allen wrench or screwdriver into the wheel's bearing hole and wiggle to let the wheel slide down.
3. Slide the wheel onto the axle.
4. Place the washer and then the nut onto the axle.
5. Repeat for all wheels.

## OUTPUT: Completed Skateboard
- Verify all parts are securely attached and there are no loose components.

## DECISION [IF]: Is the skateboard assembled correctly?
- Yes: END - The skateboard is ready to use. Go skate.
- No: RETURN to the relevant PROCESS step to correct any issues.

## END:
- The skateboard assembly process is complete.
```

instruct00501.text: Ever since Paracord and Canvas first met, they've been best friends. So, it only makes sense that they should be together, like on converses. This Instructable will show you how to switch out your lame old shoelaces for some hardcore 550 Paracord. Psst! (This is in the paracord contest... You should vote for it...If you want to, thanks!) To successfully up the cool factor of your shoes, you'll need: @ 550 Paracord, about the same size as other shoelaces. (If you're buying new paracord just for this,becauseI'm so convincing (Ha!) I would get no more than 50 feet.) You'll use about 4 feet per shoe, depending on what kind of shoe you have. @ Scissors, or a Pocketknife, if you prefer. @ A Pair of shoes (Shoelaces Optional) @ A Cigarette Lighter You'll need to measure out the paracord, to make sure that it is the same length as your shoelaces. Remember measure twice, cut once. You don't need a ruler for this, just take out one of your shoelaces and straighten it as much as you can, then put one end of the paracord next to one end of the shoelace, and wind out the paracord, and cut it at the end of the shoelace, so it is the same length as the shoelace. It doesn't have to be perfect, but close enough. Done with step 1! Achtung! There is fire involved with this step, so be careful, unless you like melted Nylon on your skin / pain. For this part, you'll want to fuse the paracord, not whip it, fusing will just make it easier to work with, and double as aglets. If you are using a brand new bundle of paracord, or are at the very end of the cord, one end will be fused already. If not, you'll just have to do this step twice. Holding near the frayed end of the paracord, but not at the very end, light it up! Wait for the inner cords to start melting. It's alright if there's a tiny flame, it will probably burn itself out, but be careful! Now, lace your shoes up any way you want, there are a myriad of instructables about just that (1,2, 3, 4, 5, 6,etc.) I laced mine up the normal way, but it's all up to you. You'll find that it helps that you fused the paracord, it makes going through the holes easier. It is a bit different using paracord, but you get used to it. Once you're done lacing your shoe, put your foot inside and tie that sucker! If you are planning on lacing both shoes with paracord, repeat this process twice. Well, now you're ready to hit the town in style, knowing that your shoes will fall apart before your shoelaces come apart! Secretly, I was planning on taking this off after I was done, and switching back to my old shoelace. But, I'm really happy with the results, and am sticking with this. Thanks for reading!!

# Structured Summary of Duct Tape Canoe Construction

## START:
- Begin the construction of a duct tape and PVC tube canoe.

## INPUT: Materials Needed for Canoe Construction
- 150 meters of 50mm duct tape
- 10x 20mm PVC pipes
- 30mm extruded foam plate
- 12x Long plastic clamps
- Saw blade (tool for cutting materials)
- Drill (for making holes in foam)

## PROCESS: Assemble the PVC Frame
- PROCESS: Align and securely assemble 5 whole PVC tubes at the ends to create the base of the canoe frame.
- PROCESS: Apply duct tape to each PVC pipe one by one to secure them together, avoiding taping them all at once to prevent slipping.
- PROCESS: Cut additional pieces of PVC tubes to spread the base tubes and give the canoe its general shape.
- PROCESS: Tape these cut pieces to the base tubes to maintain the canoe's shape.
- OUTPUT: The basic frame of the canoe is formed.

## PROCESS: Reinforce the Canoe Structure
- PROCESS: Add enough reinforcements to the frame to prevent hull deformation, focusing on areas with the main efforts:
  - The ground, due to opposing forces of mass and Archimedes' thrust.
  - The coast, where stiffness must be high due to paddle movements.
- OUTPUT: A reinforced canoe frame.

## PROCESS: Prepare and Attach the Foam
- INPUT: Cut a sheet of foam to the shape of the canoe floor and one for the back.
- PROCESS: Fasten the foam sheets to the PVC frame using long plastic clamps.
- DECISION [IF]: Does the foam rest on as many tubes as possible?
  - Yes: Proceed to the next step.
  - No: Adjust the foam placement to ensure it does not break.
- PROCESS: Drill the foam and hang it with clamps to secure it in place.
- OUTPUT: Foam secured to the canoe frame.

## PROCESS: Apply Duct Tape to Create the Shell
- PROCESS: Apply the duct tape to the canoe's frame to form the shell, ensuring the strips are straight and overlap by about 25mm.
- PROCESS: Apply two layers of duct tape, with additional strips along the length to protect the edges.
- PROCESS: Add duct tape to the top of the canoe, overlapping by about 25mm to prevent water from entering from the front and back.
- OUTPUT: The canoe is now waterproof and has a complete shell.

## OUTPUT: Final Canoe Ready for Use
- The completed duct tape and PVC tube canoe is ready for sailing.

## DECISION [IF]: Is the canoe for single-use?
  - Yes: Dispose of the canoe after use, as it is cost-effective and disposable.
  - No: Consider optimizing and storing the canoe for regular use.
  
## END:
- The process of constructing a duct tape and PVC tube canoe is complete.
```

instruct00123.title: Pallet Breaker
instruct00123.text: If you have more than a couple of pallets to break up, this tool will save a lot of time. I welded it up from scrap I had in the shop (bed frame angle iron, black pipe, square tubing, shovel handle). Lots of different scrap will work. Make sure to make your forks wide enough so you can get around a 4 inch stringer. In the beginning, if your pallet boards are too close together to fit the breaker, go ahead and knock the first one out with a hammer from behind. Bed frames and old yard tools are great raw materials. Cruise Freecycle.

instruct00430.title: Simple Metal Detector
instruct00430.text: The other day when I was searching instructables I come across on interesting and simple circuit for metal detector. It is build with 555, coil and few other components. Instructable that inspire me to do this project was this one. Main debate was: does it really work? After quick research I found this video that proof it works. That was the time when I decided to make my own metal detector. I do believe, that before you start working on metal detector you should read more about metal detectors and how they work. I am not hold responsible for any damage that occurred during reproduction. Parts: - 555 - 47 k resistor - two 22 F capacitor - PCB - 9 V battery, switch, battery cable and some wires - buzzer - 100 m of copper wire, 0,2 mm in diameter - gaffer tape and wood glue Instead of buzzer you can use 10 F capacitor and speaker (8 impendence). Tools: - breadboard and wires - pliers, tweezers, pliers for making holes - soldering iron and soldering wire - sharp knife, ruler, pencil and pair of compasses - hot glue The idea is not mine. I found schematic on this page (there is also other 499 projects with 555). I only added switch beetwen battery and circuit and instead of speaker I am using a buzzer. The most difficult part is making coil. In great help was web calculators for air coils. With them, I calculated that with coil 90 mm width I need about 250 windings and with diameter 70 mm 290 windings that inductance can be 10 mH. You can also buy already made coils online. I made coils core from cardboard. Coil is made from lacquered copper wire which is 0,2 mm in diameter. I did 260 turns. Before soldering, you must clean up both ends of coil. You can do that with help of sandpaper. I made circuit on breadboard because I didn't want when PCB would be finished it wouldn't work. You can see test in video bellow. Test was a success. Because of that I made PCB. I made it the same way that I made PCB in this project. I wanted, that final product would look nice. Therefore I decided to make handle from cardboard. Handle holds battery, switch, circuit and coil. First, I made a sketch. There were no measurements. First I made three pieces that will end up a handle. Second task was to cut out openings for batteries and for switch. Then I glued handle together will wood glue and left it to dry for 12 hours (through the night). When glue has dried I punched a hole into section where switch will be. That hole is for wires to get through. Last but not list thing to do was to glue coil to the handle. I have done that with help of hot glue. I made all components in previous steps. And now it's time to put them all together. As first I glued in switch with hot glue, then I put in battery and at last I glued in PCB with hot glue. After that I made all the required connections and put metal detctor to the test! I put finished metal detector to the test: This detector is really very simple one. But I must make a note that it is not meant for serious work. When I tested it outside, it didn't work propperly. But it is a simple and fun project for beginers. I must say I had a great time making it and using it! I wish you good luck with making this metal detector and have fun while using it.

# Metal Detector Construction System

## Summary
This system describes the process of creating a simple metal detector using a 555 timer IC, a coil, and other electronic components. The detector's design is based on a schematic found online, and it includes a switch, a buzzer, and a PCB. The most challenging part is constructing the coil, which requires precise windings for the correct inductance. The system also covers the assembly of a cardboard handle that houses the battery, switch, circuit, and coil. The final product is not intended for serious detection tasks but serves as an educational project for beginners.

## System Steps

### START:
- Begin the process of creating a simple metal detector.

### INPUT: Gather Parts and Tools
- Parts needed:
  - 555 timer IC
  - 47k resistor
  - Two 22µF capacitors
  - PCB (Printed Circuit Board)
  - 9V battery with switch, cable, and wires
  - Buzzer (or a 10µF capacitor and speaker with 8Ω impedance for alternative)
  - 100 meters of copper wire (0.2 mm in diameter)
  - Gaffer tape and wood glue
- Tools required:
  - Breadboard and jumper wires
  - Pliers, tweezers, and hole-making pliers
  - Soldering iron and solder
  - Sharp knife, ruler, pencil, and compasses
  - Hot glue gun

### PROCESS: Research and Understand Metal Detectors
- Conduct research on how metal detectors work to better understand the project.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the schematic and proof of concept available?
- IF Yes: Proceed with the project.
- IF No: Do not start the project.

### PROCESS: Create the Coil
- Use web calculators to determine the number of windings needed for the desired inductance (10mH).
- Craft the coil's core from cardboard.
- Wind the lacquered copper wire 260 times around the core.
- Clean the ends of the coil with sandpaper.

### PROCESS: Assemble the Circuit on Breadboard for Testing
- Follow the schematic to assemble the metal detector circuit on a breadboard.
- Add a switch between the battery and circuit.
- Use a buzzer instead of a speaker.

### DECISION [IF]: Does the breadboard circuit work?
- IF Yes: Proceed to create the PCB.
- IF No: Troubleshoot and retest until it works.

### PROCESS: Create the PCB
- Transfer the circuit from the breadboard to a PCB, following the same layout.

### PROCESS: Construct the Handle
- Sketch the design of the handle without specific measurements.
- Cut cardboard pieces to form the handle.
- Cut openings for the battery and switch.
- Glue the handle together with wood glue and allow it to dry for 12 hours.

### PROCESS: Assemble the Metal Detector
- Punch a hole in the handle for the switch wires.
- Glue the coil to the handle with hot glue.
- Secure the switch, battery, and PCB in the handle with hot glue.
- Make all necessary electrical connections.

### OUTPUT: Test the Metal Detector
- Conduct a test to ensure the metal detector functions correctly.

### DECISION [IF]: Does the metal detector function properly in testing?
- IF Yes: The metal detector is ready for use.
- IF No: Troubleshoot and retest.

### PROCESS: Evaluate the Metal Detector's Capabilities
- Acknowledge that the metal detector is a simple model not meant for serious use.

### END:
- Conclude the metal detector construction process.

# Summary Representation of Hair Colour Change in Photoshop

## START:
- Begin the process to change hair color in Photoshop.

## INPUT: Select a suitable photo
- Choose a photo with minimal stray hairs.
- Preferably select a photo with light-colored hair (e.g., blonde).

## PROCESS: Mask out the hair
- Select the brush tool.
- Press "Q" to enter Quick Mask mode.
- Carefully mask all the hair.
- Press "Q" again to exit Quick Mask mode.

## PROCESS: Invert the selection
- Press "Control-Shift-I" to invert the selection.

## PROCESS: Create a new layer
- Make a new layer above the background layer.
- Ensure the new layer is selected.

## INPUT: Choose a new hair color
- Select a color from the color selection panel.
- In this example, a dark red is chosen.

## PROCESS: Fill the selection with the new color
- Select the paint bucket tool.
- Fill the selected area on the new layer with the chosen color.

## PROCESS: Change layer blending mode
- Go to the layer menu.
- Change the blending mode to "Soft Light" from the overlay pull-down menu.

## PROCESS: Deselect the current selection
- Press "Control-D" to deselect.

## DECISION [IF]: Check if hair color is as desired
  - [YES]: Proceed to clean up the image.
  - [NO]: Adjust the color or blending mode and recheck.

## PROCESS: Clean up the image
- Select the eraser tool with a feathered brush.
- Erase any excess color not on the hair.

## OUTPUT: Finalized hair color change
- Review the updated image to ensure quality.

## END:
- The process of changing hair color in Photoshop is complete.

instruct00540.title: Frankenstein Finger Cookies
instruct00540.text: These gross, scary and nutty cookies will be the hit of your Halloween party! Watch your guests feast on these delicious fingers covered with crusty coconut knuckle hair, rotten almond fingernail and a frosted bloody stump. Simple and fun to make with your little ghouls. Ingredients: 1 1/4 Cup Sugar 1 Cup Butter 1 Egg 1 Egg yolk 1 tsp Coconut Extract (optional) 1 tsp Vanilla Extract 2 1/2 Cup All-Purpose Flour 1 tsp Baking Powder (not baking soda as pictured) 1/4 tsp Salt 1/2 Cup Chopped Nuts (I used Pecans) Shredded Coconut Whole Raw Almonds Green Food Dye Red Gel Frosting Equipment: Stand or Hand Mixer and Bowl Medium Bowl Sifter Cookie Sheet Parchment Paper Spatula Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Cream butter and sugar until light and fluffy. Add egg and egg yolk, vanilla and coconut extract. Mix well. Stir in nuts and green food dye. In a separate bowl, sift together the flour, baking powder, and salt. Add flour mixture to creamed mixture. Stir to blend well. If dough is too runny, add flour gradually until thickened. Also chilling the dough makes for easy shaping and less spreading in the oven. Thanks everyone for your great comments and pictures! Check out some of the comments below to see other tips for this recipe! Shape dough into 3-4 inch tapered rolls. Pinch a knuckle in the center of the roll. Place rolls onto a cookie sheet lined with parchment paper or sprayed with non-stick spray. Press an almond into the pointed end and add coconut to knuckles. Refrigerate extra dough wrapped in cling wrap between batches. Bake for 10-15 minuites or until coconut is toasted and cookie is slightly golden. Cool on a rack. Dip flat end of cookie into red gel frosting and enjoy!

instruct00037.title: Vegan Lip Balm
instruct00037.text: This quick and easy lip balm recipe with have you smiling in no time!Create your own all natural, bee-free lip balms so that you will never need to be seen with less than kissably-soft, smooth lips.(But if you're a beekeeper, or just a big fan of beeswax, it can easily be substituted in!) 1oz hard wax (candelilla, soy, etc)1 oz solid-at-room-temperature oil (coconut oil, avocado oil, mango butter, or shea butter).75 additional hard-at-room-temperature oil (cocoa butter, floral waxes, or palm oil)2 oz liquid oil (jojoba oil or olive oil) (not shown)few drops of Vitamin E Oil (Tocopherol)Essential oils (optional, your choice) - maximum 8 drops for each lip balm ToolsMicrowave-safe cup or bowl with pour spoutDigital scale sensitive to at least .1 oz (a postage scale will usually work for this)Stirring spoonFunnel that will fit opening of tubes/canistersLip balm tubes/canisters Measure your wax with your scale (not pictured).Add wax to your microwave safe container and melt on high heat in 30 second bursts.Stir between nukings and continue until the wax is completely liquified. Stir the mixture while you add all of your oils - I used coconut, jojoba, vitamin E and essential oils for a lovely scent!If the wax starts to harden while you're still mixing in ingredients, just zap it in the microwave for another 30 seconds and stir! This is the hardest part, I think, and if you have access to a pipette or a dropper, that would probably work out much better!I used a funnel that fit exactly into my little tubes. Pour the mixture slowly into your containers, tapping a bit to remove any trapped air.If the resulting product cracks, it means you're pouring it while it's too hot - let it cool a bit and try again! Come up with your own special label to let all your friends know this is something awesome that you made and couldn't wait to share with them!(hopefully you'll come up with something cooler than I did)This project is so quick and easy, I know you'll love getting all your friends involved!Enjoy :D

# Structured Summary of DIY Lip Balm Recipe

## Ingredients and Tools Input
- INPUT: Hard wax (1oz) - candelilla, soy, etc.
- INPUT: Solid-at-room-temperature oil (1oz) - coconut oil, avocado oil, mango butter, or shea butter.
- INPUT: Additional hard-at-room-temperature oil (.75oz) - cocoa butter, floral waxes, or palm oil.
- INPUT: Liquid oil (2oz) - jojoba oil or olive oil.
- INPUT: Vitamin E Oil - a few drops.
- INPUT: Essential oils (optional) - up to 8 drops per lip balm.
- INPUT: Tools - Microwave-safe cup or bowl with pour spout, digital scale, stirring spoon, funnel, lip balm tubes/canisters.

## Process of Making Lip Balm
START: Begin lip balm creation process.

### Measuring and Melting the Wax
- PROCESS: Measure the wax using a digital scale.
- PROCESS: Place wax in a microwave-safe container.
- PROCESS: Melt wax in microwave on high heat in 30-second intervals.
- PROCESS: Stir between intervals until wax is completely liquified.

### Mixing Oils
- PROCESS: Stir the mixture while adding all oils (solid-at-room-temperature oil, additional hard oil, liquid oil, Vitamin E oil, and optional essential oils).
- DECISION [IF]: Is the wax starting to harden during mixing?
  - YES: PROCESS: Microwave for another 30 seconds and stir.
  - NO: Continue to next step.

### Pouring Into Containers
- PROCESS: Use funnel to pour mixture into lip balm tubes/canisters slowly.
- PROCESS: Tap containers to remove any trapped air.
- DECISION [IF]: Does the product crack after pouring?
  - YES: PROCESS: Let it cool slightly before trying to pour again.
  - NO: Continue to next step.

### Labeling (Optional)
- PROCESS: Create and apply a custom label to the lip balm containers.

OUTPUT: Finished lip balm ready for use.

END: Lip balm creation process is complete.
```

instruct00800.title: Control Lights in Your House With Your Computer
instruct00800.text: Have you ever wanted to control the lights in your house from your computer? It's actually fairly affordable to do so. You can even control sprinkler systems, automatic window blinds, motorized projection screens, etc. You need two pieces of hardware to get started. A controller, which connects to your computer; and a dimmer switch. I'm using SmartHome Insteon products in this example. Follow the instructions provided on how to install the switch. The switch I'm using is Insteon brand, but there are other types of remote controllable switches such as X10. These switches require the neutral line to send signals (commands) over. If your switch box doesn't have a neutral, you're in trouble. Try contacting an electrician to see what you can do. You need a controller which will send commands over the power lines to your switch. I'm using the Insteon PowerLinc Controller with a Serial connection. This works with Windows and Mac. Windows has freeware easily found on Google.Setup was easy. I plugged it into the wall outlet, plugged the serial connector to my PC, and that's it.You need to download and install SDM SmartHome Device Manager. Now, once you've installed this, you can start sending commands to the PLC (PowerLinc Controller).Since I had a MacBook in another room, I installed SDM Socket Server, which is freeware for Windows. This let me connect over TCP/IP from upstairs and send messages downstairs. Note: you need to edit a registry setting to make this software work with the Serial (COM1) port. HKEY_USERS\.DEFAULT\Software\Smarthome\SmarthomeDeviceManagerThe port needed to be changed from USB4 to COM1.Here are some various programs you might also find useful. I made a Python script that basically just connects to the SDM socket server and sends messages to the PLC Controller downstairs. You can do fun stuff like flashing the lights on and off. A more practical thing to do is setting it on a timer to wake you up in the morning. Actually, you can program timers into the PowerLinc Controller directly if you use InHomeFre or other software.You have a little more control when you code the script yourself.

# Home Automation System Using SmartHome Insteon Products

## System Overview
This system allows the user to remotely control home devices such as lights, sprinkler systems, blinds, etc., via a computer. The system requires a controller connected to the computer and a dimmer switch installed in the home. The example focuses on SmartHome Insteon products.

## System Requirements
- Insteon Controller (e.g., PowerLinc Controller with Serial connection)
- Insteon Dimmer Switch
- Computer with Windows or Mac OS
- Software: SDM SmartHome Device Manager, SDM Socket Server (for Windows), and optional Python for scripting

## Process Steps

### START:
1. Ensure you have the necessary hardware: Insteon Controller and Dimmer Switch.

### PROCESS: Installation of Dimmer Switch
2. Follow the provided instructions to install the Insteon Dimmer Switch.
   - INPUT: Insteon Dimmer Switch

instruct00797.title: Easiest Cupboard Pan Lid Organiser
instruct00797.text: Haters of messy pan cupboards everywhere... rejoice! This quick cupboard door modification will leave you with more time to enjoy cooking dinner and sipping wine and less time searching for that elusive pan lid that's hidden itself inside your deepest stock pot or slipped down behind that slow cooker you've never used.Don't have a local pound/dollar store to buy sticky hooks?? Try these from Amazon!I first did a similar hack a few years ago whilst a student. Finding pan lids annoyed me as much then as it does now and so after seeing a very elegant solution on Instructables, I set out to make it even simpler. Having moved house several times since then, I was impressed when a friend improved on my previous idea, at which point I realised my current house has the same problem... PAN LIDS EVERYWHERE. iceng's uses the existing fixings in the cupboard, which made me think, can there be an even simpler solution? And, since my cupboard fixings were in the wrong place for his hack, here we are. Cheap and easily available sticky hooks. You will need.... *drum roll* ... sticky hooks and a pencil! That is it. I found these 16 hooks for 1 in a pound store. Be sure to choose ones that aren't too small. Hold up your selection of pan lids against the cupboard door. Things you may want to consider are whether the bottom one will stick out too far into your cupboard and interfere with objects sitting on the bottom shelf. Position it high enough that it won't do this. When you think you've got a good layout, hold a pan lid up against the cupboard door and draw a mark in pencil at the 4 o'clock and 8 o'clock. If you draw them too close to 3 and 9 it will fall out, if you draw them too close to 5 and 7 it might not be so stable. Peel the tabs off the stick pad and slap the hooks on the door with the hooks pointing to the approximate center of where the pan will be. No need to be too precise here. We're done. It's that simple! Enjoy your newly less hectic pan cupboard.

instruct00379.title: Homemade Dry Shampoo
instruct00379.text: I love dry shampoo, but I feel like I run out of the aerosol stuff so quickly! I've been using cornstarch as a homemade dry shampoo for years. I remember reading about it in a teen magazine when I was young - I also tried baby powder, but that went badly and I smelled funny. In the past 4-5 years, I've been adding cocoa to my homemade dry shampoo so that it blends in better with my darker hair. Baking soda is another newer addition - I like it because it can help cut down on the "greasy" smell hair can get after a couple days.This homemade dry shampoo recipe is a great substitute for the aerosol versions if the strong smells bother you, too. I'm not a big fan of walking around smelling like alcoholic fruit or candy, and I'm sure you're not either. ;)I've included a homemade dry shampoo recipe for both light and dark hair - it will make enough for tons of uses and you can fit it in a spice jar. And it gives thin, straight hair great texture - it ends up feeling thicker! cornstarch baking soda cocoa powder - just make sure it's unsweetened! Sweetened cocoa powder will turn your hair into a sticky mess.a paper funnel a container to store it in measuring spoons I've also heard of people adding essential oils to the mix, but I've never done it so I can't tell you how that will end up. :D This is the recipe you'll use if you have light hair or if you don't have any cocoa powder on hand: 1/4 cup cornstarch 1 tablespoon baking soda Combine the cornstarch and baking soda in a container and shake shake shake. Ta-daaaa! Enough dry shampoo for tons of uses. As long as you keep it sealed up, you can store it in the bathroom with no issues. I have really dark hair, so this is my go-to recipe. You can add more or less cocoa powder as needed - I use two tablespoons every time: 1/4 cup cornstarch 1 tablespoon baking soda 2 tablespoons cocoa powder Mix everything together in a small jar and you're ready to go. Special bonus with this one: smelling like chocolate. :D Just be careful that you you don't add so much cocoa powder that it gets really dark - you need to keep the amount of cocoa powder less than the amount of cornstarch and baking soda, otherwise the heat from your hands and head can warm the cocoa powder and create a melty mess. This part is easy, but you need to have a light hand when using this version of dry shampoo. Here's how I normally do it: Shake a small amount of dry shampoo out into your hand - no more than 1/2 teaspoon. I do more of a 1/4 teaspoon. Rub your hands together to disperse the dry shampoo Pat the areas of your hair that you'd like to shampoo - I tend to focus on my bangs and the very top Tousle your hair with your fingers and rub in the dry shampoo as best you can - you'll want to get pretty rough to get it all in! Brush if you still see any spots of dry shampoo And you're done! Enjoy! :D

# Homemade Dry Shampoo Recipe System

## Inputs:
- Cornstarch
- Baking soda
- Unsweetened cocoa powder (optional, for dark hair)
- Container with lid (e.g., spice jar)
- Paper funnel (for transferring ingredients)
- Measuring spoons
- Essential oils (optional, not covered in this system)

## Outputs:
- Homemade dry shampoo for light hair
- Homemade dry shampoo for dark hair

## Process:

### START:
- Begin the process of creating homemade dry shampoo.

### PROCESS: Prepare the Workspace and Ingredients
- Gather all ingredients and tools needed for the recipe.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the dry shampoo for light hair or dark hair?
- IF 'Yes', proceed to the recipe for light hair.
- ELSE, proceed to the recipe for dark hair.

### PROCESS (Light Hair Recipe):
- INPUT: Measure 1/4 cup of cornstarch.
- INPUT: Measure 1 tablespoon of baking soda.
- USE: Place a paper funnel into the container.
- PROCESS: Combine the cornstarch and baking soda through the funnel into the container.
- PROCESS: Seal the container and shake well to mix the ingredients.

### OUTPUT:
- Homemade dry shampoo for light hair is ready for storage and use.

### PROCESS (Dark Hair Recipe):
- INPUT: Measure 1/4 cup of cornstarch.
- INPUT: Measure 1 tablespoon of baking soda.
- INPUT: Measure 2 tablespoons of unsweetened cocoa powder (adjust the amount as needed, ensuring it is less than the amount of cornstarch and baking soda to prevent a melty mess).
- USE: Place a paper funnel into the container.
- PROCESS: Combine the cornstarch, baking soda, and cocoa powder through the funnel into the container.
- PROCESS: Seal the container and shake well to mix the ingredients.

### OUTPUT:
- Homemade dry shampoo for dark hair is ready for storage and use.

### PROCESS: How to Use the Dry Shampoo
- PROCESS: Shake a small amount of dry shampoo (up to 1/2 teaspoon) into your hand.
- PROCESS: Rub your hands together to disperse the dry shampoo.
- PROCESS: Pat the dry shampoo onto the desired areas of your hair, focusing on areas like bangs and the top of the head.
- PROCESS: Tousle and rub the dry shampoo into your hair vigorously to ensure it is well distributed.
- DECISION [IF]: Are there visible spots of dry shampoo remaining?
  - IF 'Yes', use a brush to remove visible spots.
  - ELSE, no further action needed.

### OUTPUT:
- Hair is refreshed and texturized without the use of aerosol products.

### STORE/DATABASE SUBROUTINE:
- Ensure the container with homemade dry shampoo is sealed and stored in a dry place, such as a bathroom cabinet.

### END:
- The process of creating and using homemade dry shampoo is complete.
```

instruct00689.title: 3 Steps & Most EFFECTIVE Way to Insulate Your Garage Door to Reduce Heat Gain
instruct00689.text: Insulating a garage door is worthwhile for many reasons. The main reason someone might want to insulate the garage is simply because they spend time in there. Be it woodworking, automotive tinkering or lifting weights on a home gym - these are all reasons why you would want the garage to be more comfortable when you're inside it. Opening a window or running a fan can help move air, but it won't stop heat from coming in so it does little toward creating a comfortable space. We are going to show you the method that is hands-down the easiest way insulate the garage door (the main culprit in heat gain) so you can be closer to a more comfortable space for whatever you're doing in there. Bonus: creating a more comfortable space for a garage that is attached to the house can usually mean the room on the other side of the garage is a bit more comfortable too! For this installation you will need the following items:4 sheets* of foil-faced foam board (pictured here is Perma"R" brand but there are several other brands available such as Johns Mansville, TUFF-R or you can make your own foil-faced foam board at home.) A knife/blade to cut the foam board A measuring tape or metal yardstick*4 sheets of 8' x 4' foil-faced foam board will generally be enough to do a standard 2 car garage door. After you have gathered all your materials, measure the size of each panel frame in the door (the metal that frames the panel). Then, add about an inch to the shorter dimensions and cut the foil-faced foam board into the rectangles. The reason you add an inch to the height of the rectangle is because you want the panels to be slightly larger than the actual framing on the door so that they are convex and curve outward when you put them in. This step is absolutely critical because if you don't create the air gap, then the foil will NOT work as a radiant barrier and you'll just be wasting your time. You can read why the radiant barrier foil requires an air gap to work, so if you just put the foam in flush against the door this method is not nearly as effective as if you create the air gap. Remember, this method is to primary reduce summer heat gain. There will be some benefit in reducing heat loss, but the big impact it to reduce heat from the sun beating down on the door.When it's time to place the foam board into the frames, situate the foam so the foil side is facing the garage door and the small air space you created from the convex shape. Start by inserting the top edge in first, then "pop" in the bottom edge. The panels should be convex and have a curve outward that is visible when you look at them from the side (see the image above). Continue repeating step 2 for the rest of the panels. Tip: save yourself the headache of wasted materials and measure each panel individually, you can't always assume they will all be the exact same size! When you're done, you'll have the benefit of a radiant barrier as your first line of defense right after the metal door, and then you'll have the foam board to help slow down the little heat that makes it past the foil. The result? A brighter, more comfortable garage door that is properly insulated to help you keep radiant heat out in the summer.
instruct00689.summary:
```markdown
# Garage Door Insulation System

## Summary Representation

```
START: Begin the process of insulating the garage door.

INPUT: Gather materials required for insulation.
- 4 sheets of 8' x 4' foil-faced foam board
- A knife/blade to cut the foam board
- A measuring tape or metal yardstick

PROCESS: Measure each panel frame on the garage door.
- Measure the size of each panel frame
- Add approximately one inch to the shorter dimension for each measurement

DECISION [IF]: Is the foam board measured and cut to the correct size?
- Yes: Proceed to the next step
- No: Re-measure and cut the foam board accurately

PROCESS: Cut the foil-faced foam board into rectangles based on the measurements taken.
- Ensure the cut rectangles are slightly larger than the actual framing for convex shape

DECISION [IF]: Is the air gap critical step understood?
- Yes: Proceed to installation
- No: Review the importance of the air gap for the radiant barrier to function

PROCESS: Install the foam board into the garage door panels.
- Position the foam board with the foil side facing the garage door
- Insert the top edge first, then "pop" in the bottom edge
- Confirm the panels are convex and curve outward

PROCESS: Repeat the installation for all panels.
- Measure each panel individually to avoid waste

OUTPUT: Insulated garage door with a radiant barrier and foam board.

END: Finish the insulation process.
```

## Detailed Step-by-Step Representation

```
START: Begin insulating the garage door.

INPUT: Collect all necessary materials for insulation.

PROCESS: Measure the existing panel frames on the garage door.
- Use the measuring tape or yardstick to get the dimensions of each panel frame.
- Add about one inch to the shorter dimension of each measurement to allow for an air gap.

DECISION [IF]: Have all the foam board pieces been measured and cut to the correct sizes?

instruct00053.text: A extruder is useful for making fast coils of clay, handles, and decorative parts. most extruders come in two types, a wall mount (instructable in progress) and todays project, a easy and simple Clay Gun. insers the prepared tube, fill with soft clay, and crank the handle.... just like a plydough machine.... on;ly more useful..... this clay gun cost under 10$ and makes enough tubes for 3 diffrent die heads, though the parts are cheap enohugh to make a bunch. the parts: you will need: a caulk gun frame- I picked up this one for 4.95 at the local hardware store- this is a 13 inch gun, designed to use the "regular" sized tubes of glue and caulk a length of 1 1/2 inch schedule 40 PVC Pipe, this peice is 5 foot long and cost $2.30 1 1/2 inch caps to use as die heads i bout 4 at 70 cents a peice 1 1/2 inch test cap this was 35 cents for 2. you will also need a marker, a hacksaw with a sharp blade and a mesuring device. measure the pipe from one end and cut off a 8 inch peice drive one of the caps onto the pipe. this one ive cut 3 holes in the cap with a knife. I could have gotten cleaner results with a drill bit. keep the holes smaller than about 1 inch in diameter, (YMMV). this pattern makes a rope if you twist the clay as it extrudes... the test cap will bethe back seal forthe gun piston. trim off the outer flange so you only have a cup shaped peice. add a glob of glue (liquid nails) and glue to the piston head of the caulk frame. let dry for a hour or so. you make have to trim the caps or pipe to make fit.. a sanding block or a rasp works well for this. Finished- to load the gun, roll a ball of clay between your hand to make a 1 inch rope. insert the rope into the sylinder, and load 'er up! start sqeezin! this gun is also useful if you want toextrude materials you cant get in tubes- like stucco or plaster of paris..the gun tubes are cheap enough to bedisposable.... to clean, just pop off thecaps and wash out, or just chuck it into a bucketof water until its ready to be used again... instruct00412.title: How to Make a Paracord Fender Keychain
instruct00412.text: For those who don't know, a fender is a bumper used mainly on boats to keep the boat from being damaged from bumping into objects. While this isn't an actual fender, it serves as a great decorative keychain. 3- Strands of paracord that are 40 inches long will create a keychain that is four inches tall (loop included) Scissors (any instrument that will cut the cord will work) Lighter Ruler or Tape Measure (I prefer to use a yardstick) Masking Tape (any tape that will stick and hold to the paracord) If you want to create a keychain that is exactly like the one shown, the loop will need to be 3 inches long once braided and will require 4 inches of cord to create the loop. Gather the three strands together and then measure from one end down to 17 inches. Hold the three strands at the 17 point, and then grab a strip of tape to secure the paracord together (make sure to place the tape edge against the 17 point). To start braiding, bring the outermost right-hand strand over the strand to its left. Then bring the outermost left-hand strand over the strand to its right. Continue this process of right-to-left until the braid length is 3 inches long and then tape the strands together to hold them in place at the point you just measured. Note: to show the directions clearly, I braided the loop loosely, to make a nice looking loop you will need to braid the strands together much tighter than shown. Bring both taped ends together forming a loop; secure them together with a strip of tape. From the top of the strip of tape (the loop end), measure down 2 inches and then secure the strands with tape at that point. The knot used to tie the fender is called a Crown Sinnet and can make a great looking decorative design to wrap objects in paracord. I. From the bottom of the tape, bring the strands back up towards the loop. II. To tie the Crown Sinnet, make a backward "C" from each strand laying each strand on top of its neighbor to the left. III. Pull the strands tight. IV. Repeat the same procedure laying each strand on top of its neighbor to the left. V. Pull the strands tight. VI. Continue as with the previous steps laying each strand on top of the strand to the left. VII. Pull the strands tight. VIII. Continue these steps until you reach the top of the tape You can finish the fender a few different ways, but with this example I chose to tie a Footrope Knot. Captain Charles Smith said this about tying the knot: "First a Crown, then a Wall, Tuck Up, and that's all". Start tying the Footrope Knot by tying a Wall Knot. It's the same as a Crown except instead of going on top of its neighbor, it goes under it. Once you've tied the Wall Knot you need to finish the knot off by tucking the strand up and behind the strands as shown with the arrow. Keep tucking each strand until you've tucked every strand. To finish the fender you will need to remove the remainder of the excess strands. Use the scissors to trim the excess paracord as close as possible to the inner part of the Footrope Knot. Now take a lighter and singe the ends of the paracord strands. Continue trimming and singing each strand until every strand is complete. NOTE: I took great care to make this tutorial as clear and easy to follow as possible, but if you get stuck on something please leave a comment and I will try to help as soon as possible. For more decorative paracord knot designs and tutorials, visit my blog.

# Fender Keychain System

## Inputs
- 3 strands of paracord, each 40 inches long
- Scissors
- Lighter
- Ruler or Tape Measure
- Masking Tape

## Outputs
- A decorative fender keychain

## Process Steps

### START
- Begin with 3 strands of paracord, each 40 inches long.

### PROCESS: Preparation
- INPUT: Measure 17 inches from one end of the paracord strands.
- STORE: Hold the strands together at the 17-inch mark.
- PROCESS: Secure the strands together with masking tape at the 17-inch mark, ensuring the tape's edge aligns with the mark.

### PROCESS: Braiding the Loop
- PROCESS: Start braiding by bringing the rightmost strand over the strand to its immediate left.
- PROCESS: Then bring the leftmost strand over the strand to its immediate right.
- DECISION [IF]: Is the braid length 3 inches?
  - Yes: Proceed to the next step.
  - No: Continue braiding.
- OUTPUT: Once the braid is 3 inches, tape the strands together to hold the braid in place.

### PROCESS: Forming the Loop
- PROCESS: Bring both taped ends together to form a loop.
- PROCESS: Secure the loop ends together with a strip of tape.

### PROCESS: Measuring for the Crown Sinnet
- INPUT: Measure 2 inches down from the top of the loop tape.
- PROCESS: Secure the strands with tape at the 2-inch mark.

### PROCESS: Tying the Crown Sinnet
- PROCESS: Bring the strands back up towards the loop.
- PROCESS: Start tying the Crown Sinnet by making a backward "C" with each strand, laying it on top of its neighbor to the left.
- PROCESS: Pull the strands tight.
- DECISION [IF]: Have you reached the top of the tape?
  - Yes: Proceed to tying the Footrope Knot.
  - No: Continue with the Crown Sinnet steps.

### PROCESS: Tying the Footrope Knot
- PROCESS: Start by tying a Wall Knot, which is similar to a Crown but goes under its neighbor instead of over.
- PROCESS: Finish the knot by tucking each strand up and behind the strands as indicated.

### PROCESS: Finalizing the Fender
- PROCESS: Trim the excess paracord as close as possible to the knot.
- PROCESS: Use a lighter to singe the ends of the paracord strands.
- PROCESS: Continue trimming and singing each strand until the fender is complete.

### OUTPUT
- The final output is a completed decorative fender keychain.

### END
- The process ends after completing the fender and ensuring all strands are trimmed and singed.

instruct00243.title: Homemade Bread Recipe
instruct00243.text: I love making homemade bread for my family. It's definitely cheaper than buying it, it's more nutritious, and I know exactly what goes in it. Plus, it stays fresh for about three 3 days in the pantry, a week in the refrigerator, and as long as you want if you freeze it. I like to bake 3 or 4 loaves at a time because it's the same work as baking one loaf. I keep one loaf for the week and I freeze the others. When i need bread, I just take it from the freezer, microwave it for two minutes, and I have bread that smells and tastes like it's just out from the oven. I am experienced making bread and these are the ingredients and measurements I came up with to make the perfect bread. This is what you need for 1 loaf of bread:3 cups of flour(any kind is fine. I use all purpose flour)3 tsp active dry yeast3 tsp sugar1 tsp salt1 cup of warm water1tbsp butter (or margarine)1 egg If you have a Kitchen Aid Mixer, that's great and it will do the work for you. But if you don't, it's ok too. You can mix everything by hand and it will turn just fine. Since I have a mixer, I will be using that with dough attachment.Start by putting the flour, yeast, sugar and the salt in the mixing bowl and combine at a low speed. Slowly pour in a cup of warm water until you make a nice consistent dough. You don't want the dough to be too soft, but if you by mistake end up pouring too much water, don't worry, it happens all the time. Just add some more flour. Before you finish, cut the butter into small cubes and mix it into the dough.When you're done mixing and the dough is a bit sticky but not significantly sticking to your hands, start kneading it with a pinch of flour and shape it into a ball. Finally, put the dough on a well floured surface and let it rest for 10 minutes. After about 10 minutes, take the dough and roll it into a long cylinder as shown. Cut it into into two equal parts and roll it again to form two rolls that are approximately 15 inches long and as wide as your fist.Put the two rolls next to each other. Connect them at one end, and start braiding them together (over-under). Once you're done braiding, lightly grease the pan,and then slowly put the bread in. Tuck the ends underneath if needed. Take an egg and beat it. Brush it over the top of the bread to give it a nice egg wash glaze. Doing this will give your bread a nice color after it bakes. If you happen to be allergic to eggs, you can do this with oil or simply skip this step Pre-heat an oven to 350 degrees. Once up to temparature, put the bread in for 30 minutes. When it's done, take it out and let it cool at least 15 mintes before cutting into it. If you cut too early, the inside will be kind of gummy. Serve it with butter or with one of my soup recipes :), or let it cool for an hour and put into plastic bags, and freeze it for as long as you want. When you want fresh bread, take it out of the freezer and microwave it for two minutes. The butter that's in the bread will help keep the softness of the bread.Enjoy!

# Homemade Bread Making System

## Ingredients and Equipment
- Flour (3 cups, any kind, preferably all-purpose)
- Active dry yeast (3 tsp)
- Sugar (3 tsp)
- Salt (1 tsp)
- Warm water (1 cup)
- Butter or margarine (1 tbsp)
- Egg (1 for egg wash, optional)
- Kitchen Aid Mixer with dough attachment (optional)
- Mixing bowl
- Rolling pin
- Baking pan
- Brush for egg wash
- Oven
- Microwave (for reheating)

## Steps

### START:
- Gather all ingredients and equipment.

### PROCESS: Prepare Dough
- INPUT: Flour, yeast, sugar, salt into the mixing bowl.
- PROCESS: Mix at a low speed to combine dry ingredients.
- INPUT: Gradually pour in warm water.
- DECISION [IF]: Is the dough too soft?
  - [YES]: Add more flour until desired consistency is achieved.
  - [NO]: Continue to next step.
- INPUT: Butter cut into small cubes.
- PROCESS: Mix butter into the dough until well incorporated.

### PROCESS: Knead and Rest Dough
- PROCESS: Knead the dough with a pinch of flour until slightly sticky but not sticking to hands.
- PROCESS: Shape dough into a ball.
- INPUT: Place dough on a floured surface.
- OUTPUT: Let dough rest for 10 minutes.

### PROCESS: Shape the Bread
- PROCESS: Roll dough into a long cylinder.
- PROCESS: Cut cylinder into two equal parts.
- PROCESS: Roll each part into 15-inch long rolls.
- PROCESS: Braid the two rolls together, tucking ends underneath.
- INPUT: Lightly grease the baking pan.
- OUTPUT: Place braided dough into the pan.

### PROCESS: Egg Wash (Optional)
- DECISION [IF]: Are you allergic to eggs?
  - [YES]: Skip egg wash or use oil.
  - [NO]: Beat one egg and brush over the top of the bread.

### PROCESS: Bake the Bread
- PROCESS: Preheat oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit.
- OUTPUT: Bake bread for 30 minutes.

### PROCESS: Cooling
- OUTPUT: Remove bread from oven and let it cool for at least 15 minutes before cutting.

### PROCESS: Serving or Storing
- DECISION [IF]: Will you serve the bread immediately?
  - [YES]: Serve with butter or soup.
  - [NO]: Let bread cool for an hour, then store.
- DECISION [IF]: Are you storing the bread?

instruct00625.title: Origami Snowflake
instruct00625.text: Joyeux Noel!These origami snowflakes make brilliant inexpensive Christmas ornaments hang on Christmas trees, decorate on walls, windows, presents, greeting cards and anywhere you can imagine.(adapted from Snowflake by creator Dennis Walker) Any square paper / origami paper (1 paper makes 1 snowflake) Scissors Fold the paper in half twice to get crease lines. Fold one corner of the paper to the center. Fold the top flap out towards the edge. This will give you two additional crease lines. Fold the paper in half again. You should get something like the image on the left. Using the two "X"s shown as points of reference, fold flap A behind (fold along the dotted line). Turn over the paper and you should see something like image on right. Fold flap B behind, aligning the blue and red edges. You should get a heart-like shape. Cut along the blue line. Use the 2 "X"s as points of reference. We only want to keep the portion labelled A. Fold an edge of the hexagon towards the center to make a crease line. Repeat for all 6 edges. At the end of the step, you will see many crease-formed triangles within the hexagon. Fold an edge of the hexagon to the center again. Using the crease lines formed in the Step 6, fold flap A to flap B (left image). Perform the same fold pattern of folding flap A to flap B repeatedly (center image), until you get a pinwheel-like shape. On the last flap, you may encounter a slight problem of the last flap being hidden under the folds. Simply pull it out to get all 6 flaps sticking out (right image). Squash fold each flap pocket (left image). You should get something like the center image. It doesn't matter which flap goes on top, so your result may not look exactly like the image on the right. On each of these flattened pockets, fold the two blue edges toward the center dotted line. The purpose is to make crease lines for the next step. You should get something like the image on the right. Unfold the folds done in Step 9 to reveal the crease lines. For each pocket, bring the blue "X" toward the red "X". The crease lines formed in Step 9 will help. After completing all 6 pockets, the paper should look something like the image on the right. Turn the paper over (left image). Bring each pointed tip of the hexagon towards the center. Ensure that each adjacent fold exposes a tiny flap. Do not hide this flap beneath the fold. You should get something like the image on the right. Squash fold each of the tiny flaps. The crease lines formed are meant to help in the next step. Invert the folds done in Step 12, hiding the flaps neatly underneath. Flip over. Bring each tip from the middle as far out as possible and make a fold.At the end of the step, you should get 12 flaps 6 big flaps, 6 small flaps. Flip over. In between any two big flaps is a small flap. "Bring forward" each of the small flaps. Look closely at the left and center images as a guide. At the end of the step, you should get 6 kite-like shapes (image on the right). For each half of a "kite", bring the blue edge to the center of the kite (dotted). Squash-fold the pop-up towards the edge. You should get something like the image on the right. You need to perform this a total of 12 times.You're finally done! :)Visit www.yokebakery.com for more recipes and craft tutorials! :)

```markdown
# Origami Snowflake System

## Process Summary

This system represents the creation of an origami snowflake, which can be used as a Christmas ornament. The system takes square paper as an input and goes through a series of folding, cutting, and shaping steps to produce a snowflake as the output.

## Steps

### START:
- INPUT: Square paper or origami paper (1 paper makes 1 snowflake)
- INPUT: Scissors

### PROCESS: Prepare the paper
- Fold the paper in half twice to create crease lines.

### PROCESS: Create initial folds
- Fold one corner of the paper to the center to make an initial crease.
- Fold the top flap out towards the edge to create two additional crease lines.

### PROCESS: Refold and shape
- Fold the paper in half again, following the existing creases.

### PROCESS: Fold flap A
- Using the "X" marks as references, fold flap A behind along the dotted line.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the paper turned over?
- IF 'Yes', proceed to the next step.
- IF 'No', turn over the paper.

### PROCESS: Fold flap B
- Fold flap B behind, aligning the blue and red edges to form a heart-like shape.

### PROCESS: Cut the paper
- Cut along the blue line, using the 2 "X"s as points of reference, keeping portion labeled A.

### PROCESS: Create hexagon creases
- Fold an edge of the hexagon towards the center to make a crease line.
- OUTPUT: Crease-formed triangles within the hexagon.

### PROCESS: Fold edges to center
- Fold an edge of the hexagon to the center again, using the crease lines formed in the previous step.

### PROCESS: Create pinwheel shape
- Fold flap A to flap B using the crease lines.
- Repeat the fold pattern until a pinwheel-like shape is formed.

### PROCESS: Adjust the last flap
- Pull out the last hidden flap to have all 6 flaps sticking out.

### PROCESS: Squash fold each flap
- OUTPUT: Flattened pockets that may not look exactly like the image.

### PROCESS: Create crease lines on pockets
- Fold the two blue edges toward the center dotted line on each flattened pocket.

### PROCESS: Form the snowflake points
- Unfold the previous step's folds to reveal the crease lines.
- Bring the blue "X" toward the red "X" for each pocket, using the crease lines as a guide.

### PROCESS: Turn the paper over
- Bring each pointed tip of the hexagon towards the center without hiding the tiny flap.

### PROCESS: Squash fold tiny flaps
- OUTPUT: Crease lines for the next step.

### PROCESS: Invert folds
- Hide the tiny flaps neatly underneath by inverting the folds.

### PROCESS: Extend the tips
- Bring each tip from the middle as far out as possible and make a fold.
- OUTPUT: 12 flaps (6 big flaps, 6 small flaps).

### PROCESS: Adjust small flaps
- "Bring forward" each of the small flaps between the big flaps.

### PROCESS: Shape kite-like figures
- For each half of a "kite", bring the blue edge to the center of the kite and squash-fold the pop-up towards the edge.
- OUTPUT: 6 kite-like shapes.

### PROCESS: Complete the snowflake
- Perform the kite-like shaping step a total of 12 times.

### OUTPUT:
- The completed origami snowflake.

### END:
- The origami snowflake is now ready to be used as a Christmas ornament.
```

instruct00756.title: Embroidered Notebook Covers
instruct00756.text: This instructable combines string art, embroidery and geometry. I opted for geometric theme, but there are many other options. You can find a lot of different patterns online, just look for string art examples. To complete this project, all you need is a notebook, compass, protractor, ruler, embroidery floss or doubled thread, needle, superglue and scotch tape. If you don't want to play around with instruments, you can just print out a pattern and use it as a guide. Cut out your ready pattern and place it on top of your notebook, if you are satisfied with the placement, use few pieces of tape to secure the drawing to the cover. Open the notebook and flip it upside down, so you don't punch through pages. Use a needle, pin or protractor to create holes in appropriate spots. Thread embroidery floss through the first hole and secure the end with a dab of superglue and tape. Begin threading the rest once superglue is dry. When your embroidery is done, use the same method to secure the remaining end of embroidery floss. This one is the simplest pattern, doesn't require any tools to draw it, except for checkered paper. You can make the holes spaces as wide or as tight as you want. To embroider it properly, just follow the numbers on the chart. For this one you will need to draw a circle and mark 24 spots placed 15 apart. Then, you mark the tips of three triangles, each 120 apart from each other. Three different patterns, can be applied separately or together, one in top of another, each pattern different color. Just follow the numbers. This one is a variation of the first embroidered notebook, except it's a smaller version and has to be repeated at least 8 times. You can make it more dense and draw more arms if you want to.

## System Overview
The system is a method for creating string art embroidery on a notebook using geometric patterns. The system's input includes materials and tools such as a notebook, compass, protractor, ruler, embroidery floss or thread, needle, superglue, and scotch tape, as well as a pattern that can be drawn or printed. - The string art embroidery on the notebook is completed.

- For more complex patterns, repeat the above process with additional geometric shapes and multiple colors of floss.

instruct00316.title: New Rocket Powered Matchbox Cars! - Extreme!
instruct00316.text: First of all my inspiration for this project came from zjharva. This is a new version of Rocket Powered Matchbox cars with video! Now you see what they really do on rocket power! I used Hot Wheels cars but I felt they really needed to be called Matchbox because of what were about to do to them! First of all you will need a package of Estes A10-PT model rocket engines. You can find these at most Walmart store, hobby shops or other stores that carry model rockets. Something to attach the 'engines' to the cars. I used 32 gauge wire that you can wrap around the vehicle and secure the 'engine' safely during ignition. you need something to guide the car on it's track. Without this, the rocket shoots the car and rolls it, flipping and tumbling across the 'track'. I used a coffee stirrer and after cutting a small groove in the bottom of the car, cut it to size & glued it in place. This is the perfect diameter for the string that the car rides on. I picked up an Estes Race Controller that runs on 4 "AA" batteries and has a long enough wire with alligator clips at the end. These will attach to the rocket igniters and fire the rocket! This was wicked fun!! We brought them to a tennis court which was the perfect really flat surface and tested them out...here is the video!! Enjoy!

# Comprehensive Structured Summary of Rocket Powered Matchbox Cars Project

## System Overview
The system described is a method for converting Hot Wheels or Matchbox cars into rocket-powered vehicles using model rocket engines. ### START: Begin Project Preparation

### PROCESS: Preparing the Guide for the Cars

- PROCESS: Cut the coffee stirrer to size

### DECISION [IF]: Is the tennis court available for testing?
  - Yes: Proceed to the testing phase
  - No: Find an alternative flat surface for testing

### PROCESS: Testing the Rocket-Powered Cars
- PROCESS: Bring the modified cars to the tennis court or chosen flat surface
- PROCESS: Set up the string track for the cars to ride on
- PROCESS: Use the race controller to ignite the rocket engines

### END: Project Completion

instruct00634.title: Twist and Pop Card
instruct00634.text: Welcome back to another Paper Chaser TO tutorial! Today we'll be making one of my favourite cards, the Twist and Pop card. It's a fun, and simple card to make and I hope that you guys will enjoy making it! Once you've got the template, use it to cut your pieces, and then score the pieces.We'll be starting off with the mechanism. Get your mechanism and fold it in half like a hotdog. Make sure there's a nice crease before you unfold it. Now you'll want to fold it diagonally. When you've finished folding it diagonally, unfold it, and pinch along the middle crease. You should end up with something similar to the photo above. Grab your card piece and fold the outer edges to the center.Flip everything over and fold it in half. Make sure to press down on everything to make the crease stand out more. After you finished folding everything, you should have something similar to the photo above. Glueing down the mats is optional and not necessary for this tutorial.Now grab your card piece and fold it in half. Get your mechanism that you made in step 1 and card piece that you made in step 2.Line up the mechanism with the card piece and grab a pencil. You're going to want to use the pencil to mark down the glue spots on the card.Apply glue to the areas where you just marked with the mechanism. With the mechanism, make sure that it's pointing upwards before pushing it down onto the glue. This part is a little bit tricky. You're going to want to bend and fold the card piece with the mechanism closed.Apply glue to the top of the mechanism so that we can stick it into the card. After you stuck it onto the card, apply glue again to the top of the mechanism. After that, you'll want to close the card on the mechanism.When you open the card now, it will twist and pop open! Congratulations on making your twist and pop card!

## System Overview
The system guides the user through the process of creating a Twist and Pop card. The system consists of a series of steps involving folding, scoring, gluing, and assembling card components to achieve the final product, which is a card that twists and pops open when opened.

- PROCESS: Fold the mechanism piece diagonally.

- PROCESS: Pinch along the middle crease to create a point.

### PROCESS: Prepare Card Piece
- INPUT: Acquire the card piece.
- PROCESS: Fold the outer edges of the card piece to the center.

- OUTPUT: Mechanism stuck inside the card.

- Celebrate the creation of the Twist and Pop card.

instruct00128.title: Honeydukes' Chocolate Frogs
instruct00128.text: A "Muggle" version of Honeydukes' Chocolate Frogs. Equipment: Microwave Wooden spatula 1-2 Plastic Frog Molds* Microwave safe mixing bowl Ingredients: One 12 oz. package of semi-sweet chocolate chips One 12 oz. package of white chocolate chips Makes 24 chocolate frogs *Note: You may purchase a plastic frog mold from Amazon.com (see below) for roughly $3 plus shipping and handling.http://www.amazon.com/FROG-Animal-Candy-Mold-Chocolate/dp/B000EBMUNU Empty both of your 12 oz. chocolate chip bags into your microwavable safe bowl. Place chocolate chip filled bowl in the microwave on high for 30 seconds. After 30 seconds is up, remove the bowl and stir the chocolate chips. Repeat microwaving for 30 second intervals until chocolate is completely melted. Pour your melted chocolate into your plastic molds. Use a wooden spatula to help pour chocolate. Place molds on a flat surface in the freezer. Wait 30 minutes. Remove chocolate frogs and turn mold upside down onto a plate or other desired serving item. Your chocolate frog should easily fall out onto plate. If it doesn't, gently tap the plastic mold with two fingers until chocolate frog falls out. Now go and enjoy your magical amphibian treat!

instruct00343.title: Mouse Trap Indicator
instruct00343.text: I've been thinking for a while about how to make a mouse trap that turns ON an LED after it's set off. The reason being for all of us who have a couple traps in the basement or garage that you don't necessarily check everyday. I wanted something that would get my attention that I caught a mouse without having to go right up to it. I also wantedto do that as simple as possible (ie no arduino to post a tweet). Here's what I came up with. One of the biggest things I wanted was to make sure I used Items I already had around and were fairly common. The only exception was I did buy some mini-clothes pins instead of using a regular size one because I liked the compactness of it. And I could mount it on top. But you can use a regular one and either attach it to the bottom of the mousetrap, or the side. - An LED - Duct tape - wire - 3V battery & case (I pulled this one off an old motherboard) - clothes pin (you can get these as most major craft stores) - mouse trap Tools: - Soldering iron - glue gun - wire cutters - helping hands are a plus Cut a piece of duct tape and fold it over the action bar. I later trimmed it to about 1cm wide on the left side. That way it doesn't interfere with the trigger bar in the middle. As a side benefit, it also acts as a pull tab so you don't have to touch the mouse when releasing it from the trap. Strip about 2in off the ends of each wire and wrap them around each of the jaws of the clothes pin. I found starting the wrap with my needle-nose pliers really helped. The closed position with obviously be on. While set we'll be putting that strip of duct tape in between it to stop the current. This is basically connecting the battery to the LED through the clothes pin. Again, keeping the the theme of being as simple as possible. Connect one of the wires from the clothes pin to the positive terminal of the battery case and the other wire to the positive leg of the LED. Then connect the negative leg of the LED to the negative of the battery case. If you put your battery in now it should light up. Here I simply used my hot-glue gun and glued it to the top of the mouse trap. I wanted to use my Gorilla glue for a more secure hold, but it was dried out. And this seemed hold better than I thought. After several tests runs it was still holding great. I faced the LED out the back rather than pointed up because these mousetraps tend to flip when sprung and I wanted to make sure it was visible no matter which side it landed on. Now just put the strip of duct tape in between the jaws of the clothes pin when setting the trap. When the trap springs, the strip will be pulled out, setting the connection and the LED will turn on. That's it. Easy enough right? Of course the builder in me wants to take it to the next level. One idea I had was to make the LED blink so you're more likely to notice it. The other is to add a joule thief to the circuit so you can run it off 1 AA battery that's close to dead. But there are plenty of great instructables on those you can find. Let me know of any modifications you can think of and enjoy!

# Mouse Trap LED Alert System

## System Overview
The objective is to create a system that illuminates an LED when a mouse trap is triggered. The system should be simple, using commonly available materials and basic electronics knowledge.

### Materials and Tools Required
- INPUT: LED
- INPUT: Duct tape
- INPUT: Electrical wire
- INPUT: 3V battery & case
- INPUT: Clothes pin (mini-sized for compactness)
- INPUT: Mouse trap
- INPUT: Soldering iron (Tool)
- INPUT: Glue gun (Tool)
- INPUT: Wire cutters (Tool)
- INPUT: Needle-nose pliers (Tool, optional but helpful)
- INPUT: Helping hands (Tool, optional but beneficial)

## Step-by-Step Process

### Preparing the Mouse Trap
START: Begin the process of creating the mouse trap LED alert system.
- PROCESS: Cut a piece of duct tape and fold it over the action bar of the mouse trap.
- OUTPUT: Duct tape attached to the action bar, acting as a pull tab.

### Preparing the Clothes Pin
- PROCESS: Strip about 2 inches off the ends of two wires.
- PROCESS: Wrap the stripped ends around each jaw of the clothes pin using needle-nose pliers if available.
- OUTPUT: Wires securely attached to the clothes pin, creating a switch mechanism.

### Assembling the Circuit
- PROCESS: Connect one wire from the clothes pin to the positive terminal of the battery case.
- PROCESS: Connect the other wire from the clothes pin to the positive leg of the LED.
- PROCESS: Connect the negative leg of the LED to the negative terminal of the battery case.
- DECISION [IF]: Is the battery inserted and the clothes pin closed (completing the circuit)?
  - Yes: OUTPUT: The LED should light up.
  - No: PROCESS: Proceed without testing the LED.

### Mounting the Components
- PROCESS: Use the hot-glue gun to glue the LED and battery case to the top of the mouse trap.
- OUTPUT: LED and battery case securely attached to the mouse trap.

### Setting the Trap
- PROCESS: Insert the strip of duct tape between the jaws of the clothes pin when setting the trap.
- OUTPUT: The trap is set and the circuit is open, preventing the LED from lighting up.

### Triggering the System
- DECISION [IF]: Is the mouse trap sprung?
  - Yes: 
    - PROCESS: The strip of duct tape is pulled out as the trap springs.
    - PROCESS: The clothes pin jaws close, completing the circuit.
    - OUTPUT: The LED turns on, indicating the trap has been triggered.
  - No: PROCESS: The system remains in a waiting state, with the LED off.

### Possible Enhancements
- DECISION [IF]: Does the builder wish to enhance the system?
  - Yes:
    - PROCESS: Consider making the LED blink to increase visibility.
    - PROCESS: Add a joule thief to the circuit to use a nearly depleted AA battery.
    - STORE/DATABASE SUBROUTINE: Research additional instructables for enhancements.
  - No: END: The basic system is complete.

END: The mouse trap LED alert system is complete and operational.
```

instruct00437.title: Wooden Beer Mug
instruct00437.text: This instructable is for making a big wooden beer mug. I made it 15cm x 22cm. It is not so suitible for drinking beer (pallet wood can be toxic) but for decorative purpose or ,like me as a trash and beercaps bin. If you wanne make one you can drink from ,there are some suggestions in the comments. For this mug i used some pallet wood i had laying around. You will need 15 sticks cut at a length of 22 cm and at an angle of 12 degrees. Put the sticks around something round and tape them together ,but leave one opening. Now take the whole thing and put it on a flat surface and put some glue between the sticks . Now fold it together again. I used some rope and a pair of screwdrivers to tighten the sticks together. Now you can let the glue dry. Now you can make the ear. Mine is approx. 20cm x 8cm. I did all the sanding with an angle grinder. When the glue of the mug has dried ,you can also sand this. To make it look better i've put some rings out of sheetmetal around them. Best is to screw these behind the handle into one piece of wood. You could also use some rope to put around the mug. With the angle grinder i made some grooves and glued the rings in. Now put the ear on it , I made the mistake to put the bottom in before screwing the ear on from the inside. Next glue the bottom in and do some more sanding

instruct00466.title: DIY Force Sensitive Resistor (FSR)
instruct00466.text: Make a force sensitive resistor (a pressure sensor) with spare parts instead of spending $5 - $20 each. ToolsSoldering ironHot glue gunKnife/razorWire cutterComponentsSolderHot glueOne-sided copper PCBConductive foamWireThe foamConductive foam is what microcontrollers generally come packaged in. If you've received little ATmega microcontrollers or PICs, sometimes they'll be surrounded by conductive foam inside a little case or box. Not all conductive foam is created equal: some of it bounces back into shape faster than others. If you use PIC foam to make your FSR, it will respond quickly, but if you use ATmega foam will take a second to release. The fact that this FSR has a visible deformation is the primary difference from other FSRs. Use the knife/razor to score your PCB into two plates that mirror each other. I went with approximately one-square-inch squares, but you could do any two shapes so long as there is copper in between. Cut your foam into the same shape as the plate. Solder one wire to each plate. You'll want to make sure the solder is going to hold the wire in place, so clean the copper beforehand if necessary and use plenty of solder. Glue the three pieces together. Only glue along the outline of the FSR, otherwise it will not conduct well. For mine, I just glued the top and bottom of both plates to the foam. Grab a multimeter and measure the resistance across your FSR. Your values will vary, but I got about 200 kiloohms at rest and 9 kiloohms when almost completely depressed. If your plates have a larger surface area, or the foam in between is thinner, these values will be smaller. VariationsUse it to Dim an LED (video + code)Use it to Make some noise (video)Try different kinds of foam (test resistance across the foam first to make sure it's conductive)Cut unusual shapesTest different foam configurations (e.g.: multi-layered foam)Test different plate materials (e.g.: aluminum foil on cardboard/plastic/wood)Make humongous FSR arraysLinksSensorWiki FSR page explains FSR theory and use, with examplesProtolab explanation of FSR use in the context of other sensorsThanks to Dane Kouttron and Zach Barth for introducing this technique to me, and leaving a few FSRs around the eclub.
